Interfacing C, C++ and Fortran

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

Checked against R 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) on 2026-10-20; R 4.6.2 is scheduled for 2026-10-29. This page compiles and runs code, so besides base R it used the GNU compilers gcc and g++ 13.3 and gfortran 13.3 with GNU make (all three are in the container image), and these add-on packages: Rcpp 1.1.2 for the C++ sections, bench 1.1.4 for one benchmark, pkgbuild 1.4.8 to ask whether build tools exist, and usethis 3.2.2, devtools 2.5.2 and roxygen2 8.1.1 to put compiled code into a copy of the shelf package; lintr 3.4.0 was used only to check the R scripts. cpp11 0.5.5 is installed and is named in one sentence, not run. RcppArmadillo, RcppParallel and inline are not installed, so what the page says about them is prose, and Rtools45 on Windows and Apple’s Command Line Tools on macOS were not available either: everything said about those toolchains comes from the manuals and is marked as not run.

R is an interpreter written in C, and it was designed from the start to be extended with compiled code: a great part of base R is C and Fortran called through the same entry points described here. This page is about the other direction, the code you write yourself. It explains how a C, C++ or Fortran function becomes a shared object that R loads (R CMD SHLIB and dyn.load()), the four interfaces that call it (.Call(), .External(), .C() and .Fortran()), how C code reads and builds R objects through the SEXP type and keeps them safe from the garbage collector (PROTECT and UNPROTECT), how routines are registered so that R can check them (R_registerRoutines() and useDynLib in NAMESPACE), what goes in src/Makevars, how Rcpp reduces the C++ boilerplate, which parts of R’s C API a package may use, and what each platform needs installed. Every example was compiled and run, and the error and warning messages are the ones R printed.

Every R example is a script that was run with Rscript on R 4.6.1 with warnings printed as they happen (options(warn = 1)), and the lines that start with #> are what it printed. The scripts also pass the default lintr linters. Every C, C++ and Fortran file shown is the exact file that was compiled; it was also compiled with -Wall -pedantic set in a personal Makevars file (shown below) and gave no warning; the transcripts of the build commands show the default build. The compiler command lines R prints are long and name the container’s directories and distribution, so the page shows them with the flags shortened to the ones that matter, and omits the line that names the compiler version and the operating system; where that happens the text says so. The compiled examples use small data typed into the scripts (a handful of loan durations in days, a few ISBN strings), not the CSV files of the running scenario described on the section index, because the compiled objects live in their own directory; the package examples use the shelf package of Creating Packages, copied and extended with a src/ directory, with paths shown as ~/shelf. The shared-object extension is .so on Linux and macOS and .dll on Windows, so the scripts write paste0("add", .Platform$dynlib.ext); where the page says add.so, read add.dll on Windows.

This page links to the references for the three languages that this one calls: the C Reference (and its Build and Tooling page), the C++ Reference (and its Program Structure and Compilation page, which explains extern "C"), and the Fortran Reference, whose pages Interoperability with C and Calling Fortran from C, C++ and Python were added by issue #277 and cover the Fortran side of what is shown here from R. Measuring whether compiled code is worth writing belongs to Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking; how R stores the objects that C code receives is the subject of Memory and Copy Semantics; calling Python instead is Python Interop with reticulate.

Why leave R, and when not to

Most of R’s speed already comes from compiled code. sum(), %*%, sort(), lm() and the arithmetic on vectors all end in C or Fortran that someone else wrote and tested, so the first answer to a slow script is usually a better use of those: vectorise, avoid growing objects, choose another algorithm, or use a package such as data.table that is compiled for that job. Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking shows how to measure, and Vectorisation and Iteration covers the byte-code compiler and preallocation that make plain R loops much faster than their reputation. The manual Writing R Extensions says the same: before using .Call() or .External() it advises to consider whether interpreted code is fast enough, and whether .C() is enough, because the first two give much more control and impose much greater responsibilities (Writing R Extensions: Handling R objects in C).

There are four good reasons to write compiled code anyway.

  • A loop that cannot be vectorised. Each iteration depends on the previous one (a simulation, a recursive filter, a state machine, a dynamic-programming table), so the work cannot be handed to a built-in that operates on whole vectors.

  • An existing library. A numerical routine in Fortran, a parser in C, a geometry engine in C++: wrapping it is far cheaper than porting it. The Fortran BLAS and LAPACK page describes the libraries R itself links.

  • Memory control. R copies on modification (see Memory and Copy Semantics); compiled code can fill a preallocated buffer in place.

  • A data structure R does not have. A heap, a hash table, a trie, a spatial index, kept alive between calls behind an external pointer.

The price is real. Compiled code is the one place where a mistake does not give an R error but a crash of the whole R process, or worse, a wrong answer with no message. It needs a compiler on every machine that installs the package from source, it has to be kept in step with changes of the R C API (this page’s last sections), it is harder to debug, and it makes a package harder to get onto CRAN. The rule of thumb in the R community is to profile first, change the algorithm second, and write compiled code last; the example near the end of this page puts numbers on why.

The interfaces at a glance

Interface R side C or Fortran side Use it when

.Call()

.Call(sym, a, b), up to 65 arguments

SEXP f(SEXP a, SEXP b)

The default. Any R object in, any R object out; arguments are not copied; the function does its own type checks.

.External()

.External(sym, a, b)

SEXP f(SEXP args), one pairlist

A variable number of arguments, or the argument names (tags) matter.

.C()

.C(sym, a, b) returns a list of the modified arguments

void f(double *a, int *n), pointers only

Old code, or a routine that only reads and writes plain numeric vectors; no R headers needed.

.Fortran()

.Fortran(sym, a, b), same as .C()

subroutine f(a, n), lower-case name

Existing Fortran 77 or Fortran 90 subroutines; for modern Fortran, bind© and .C().

Rcpp attributes

an ordinary R function generated for you

a C++ function with // [[Rcpp::export]]

C++ code that wants vectors, lists and data frames as classes, with conversion and error handling generated.

Source: Writing R Extensions: System and foreign language interfaces

The rest of the page follows that order: the C route with .Call() first, because everything else is a variation of it, then .C() and .Fortran(), .External(), and finally C++ and Rcpp.

The toolchain: what R needs on each platform

R compiles C, C++ and Fortran with the compilers it was configured with, and it records the commands in etc/Makeconf inside the R installation. R CMD config prints any of those variables, and R CMD SHLIB and R CMD INSTALL read them, so the compiler is never named in your own build files. The script below asks whether R can find a working compiler (pkgbuild::has_build_tools() compiles a small C file with R CMD SHLIB, which is the real test), prints the shared-object extension of this platform, and prints the C, C++ and Fortran compiler commands R uses. On this machine the C compiler is selected with the C23 option (-std=gnu2x is gcc 13’s spelling of it) and the C++ compiler with the C++20 option, which are the defaults of R 4.5.0 and R 4.6.0 respectively; the version notes at the end of the page give the NEWS entries.

# Is there a compiler R can use? TRUE means make and a C compiler were found.
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE

# The shared-object extension of this platform.
.Platform$dynlib.ext
#> [1] ".so"

# What R was configured to compile with (the same as `R CMD config CC`).
r_bin <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "R")
for (variable in c("CC", "CXX", "FC")) {
  value <- system2(r_bin, c("CMD", "config", variable), stdout = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("%s: %s\n", variable, value))
}
#> CC: gcc -std=gnu2x
#> CXX: g++ -std=gnu++20
#> FC: gfortran

Source: R documentation: system2

The help page of has_build_tools() adds that debug = TRUE prints extra information, and that on Windows a failure such as R CMD config CC returning status 127 means that Rtools is not on the PATH (pkgbuild package documentation: has_build_tools). What has to be installed differs by platform.

Platform What to install Notes

Linux

A C compiler, a C++ compiler, a Fortran compiler and make; on Debian-based systems the build-essential and gfortran packages cover all of them, and r-base-dev brings the headers.

This is the setup of the container used for this page.

macOS

Apple’s Command Line Tools, installed with xcode-select --install, for the C and C++ compilers (Apple’s clang); a Fortran compiler is separate.

Xcode itself does not contain a Fortran compiler. The R-admin manual and the macOS tools page recommend the universal GNU Fortran 14.2 installer for current R, and say that to compile packages you must use the same Fortran that built your R, so check the download page of your R version.

Windows

Rtools45, the toolchain for R 4.5.0 and later (including R-devel), installed from the CRAN Rtools page.

Rtools45 provides GCC 14.2 (MinGW-w64) and MSYS2 build tools. Earlier R versions use Rtools44 (R 4.4.x), Rtools43, Rtools42 and Rtools40; each page of the Rtools portal lists the R versions it serves. R must be able to find it; usually the installer arranges that.

Source: R Installation and Administration: The Windows toolset

The R Installation and Administration manual describes the macOS requirement in its section on installing packages (R Installation and Administration: macOS packages), and the Fortran compiler for macOS in its appendix on building R (R Installation and Administration: Fortran compiler). The macOS tools page (Tools for macOS: mac.r-project.org) is the download page for the Fortran compiler and notes the compiler to use for each R build. The R for Windows FAQ says the way to build a DLL by hand is the same command as elsewhere: R CMD SHLIB foo.c bar.f, run with the R of the installed version (R for Windows FAQ 8.3: How do I include compiled C code?), and the Rtools portal at Rtools: Toolchains for building R and R packages from source on Windows lists which Rtools serves which R. None of the Windows or macOS steps was run for this page.

A source package that contains only R code needs none of this; the toolchain is needed only by packages with a src/ directory and by the code you compile yourself. Binary packages from CRAN (Windows and macOS) and from distribution or Posit Package Manager repositories on Linux are compiled for you, which is why many R users never install a compiler.

From C source to a loaded shared object

The smallest .Call function

A function called through .Call() takes R objects as arguments and returns one. In C, an R object of any type is a SEXP (a pointer to R’s internal node type, described in the next section), so the function takes SEXP arguments and returns a SEXP. The smallest useful function adds two numbers. Rf_asReal() coerces the first element of its argument to a C double, and Rf_ScalarReal() builds a length-one numeric vector from a double; the header Rinternals.h declares both, and R.h the rest of the common API.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

SEXP add(SEXP x, SEXP y) {
  return Rf_ScalarReal(Rf_asReal(x) + Rf_asReal(y));
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Calling .Call

R CMD SHLIB turns the source file into a shared object. It calls make with R’s own rules, so it uses the compiler, the flags and the link line recorded when R was built. The transcript shows the two commands it runs, with the flags shortened (the real lines carry the include directory of this R installation and about a dozen hardening and diagnostic flags) and without the first line it prints, which names the compiler version and the operating system.

R CMD SHLIB add.c
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -I"<R_HOME>/include" -fPIC -O2 -c add.c -o add.o
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -shared -o add.so add.o -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR

Source: R documentation: SHLIB

The first command compiles add.c into an object file; the second links the object file into add.so against libR. The options come from R CMD SHLIB --help; the transcript is the complete help except its last line, which gives the address for bug reports (the odd "alsp" in the --use-C17 line is in R’s own text).

R CMD SHLIB --help
#> Usage: R CMD SHLIB [options] files | linker options
#>
#> Build a shared object for dynamic loading from the specified source or
#> object files (which are automagically made from their sources) or
#> linker options.  If not given via '--output', the name for the shared
#> object is determined from the first source or object file.
#>
#> Options:
#>   -h, --help		print short help message and exit
#>   -v, --version		print version info and exit
#>   -o, --output=LIB	use LIB as (full) name for the built library
#>   -c, --clean		remove files created during compilation
#>   --preclean		remove files created during a previous run
#>   -n, --dry-run		dry run, showing commands that would be used
#>   --use-LTO		use Link-Time Optimization
#>   --no-use-LTO		do not use Link-Time Optimization
#>   --use-C17	        use a C standard at most C17 (alsp C90, C99)
#>   --use-C23	        use a C standard at least C23
#>
#> Windows only:
#>   -d, --debug		build a debug DLL
#>
#> [exit 0]

Source: R documentation: SHLIB

R CMD SHLIB accepts C (.c), C++ (.cc, .cpp), fixed-form Fortran (.f), free-form Fortran (.f90, .f95), Objective C and Objective C++ sources, or object files, or linker options. Files for the Fortran preprocessor (.F) are not accepted. The name of the shared object is taken from the first file unless -o is given. Two details from the manual are worth keeping in mind: make does not rebuild when only the flags changed (use --preclean), and a file named test.c next to test.f makes R CMD SHLIB test.f compile the C file instead (Writing R Extensions: Creating shared objects).

dyn.load, is.loaded and the symbol table

dyn.load() loads a shared object into the running R process, and .Call() then finds the C function by its name. The manual advises against assuming a file extension, and recommends file.path(path1, path2, paste0("mylib", .Platform$dynlib.ext)). The script loads add.so, calls the function with doubles, integers and a missing value, shows that only the first element of each argument is used (because the C code reads it with Rf_asReal()), and shows the two ways to be exact about which shared object a name belongs to: the PACKAGE argument, and a native symbol object from getNativeSymbolInfo().

# Load the shared object built by `R CMD SHLIB add.c`, then call into it.
dyn.load(paste0("add", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
is.loaded("add")
#> [1] TRUE
.Call("add", 1, 2)
#> [1] 3
.Call("add", 1L, 2L)
#> [1] 3
.Call("add", NA_real_, 2)
#> [1] NA
.Call("add", c(5, 6), c(10, 20))
#> [1] 15

# Pass PACKAGE so that the search is confined to this shared object.
add <- function(x, y) .Call("add", x, y, PACKAGE = "add")
add(0.1, 0.2) == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE
add(0.1, 0.2)
#> [1] 0.3

# The loaded objects, and the symbol as an R object.
"add" %in% names(getLoadedDLLs())
#> [1] TRUE
info <- getNativeSymbolInfo("add", PACKAGE = "add")
class(info)
#> [1] "NativeSymbolInfo"
info$name
#> [1] "add"

# Unloading is rarely needed; it lets the file be rebuilt on Windows.
invisible(dyn.unload(paste0("add", .Platform$dynlib.ext)))
is.loaded("add")
#> [1] FALSE

Source: R documentation: dyn.load

The loaded shared object is listed by getLoadedDLLs(), whose elements are named after the file without the extension. dyn.unload() removes it; the manual calls unloading unnecessary and not safe in general, but needed on some platforms (Windows) to allow the DLL to be rebuilt. Unloading a DLL and reloading a rebuilt one with the same name may not work on every platform (Writing R Extensions: dyn.load and dyn.unload). In practice, when you edit a C file during development, restart R after rebuilding, or use pkgload::load_all() (below), which handles unloading for a package.

PACKAGE matters more than it looks. A bare .Call("add", x, y) asks R to search every loaded shared object, and R’s search order is most recently loaded first; if two packages define a C function called add, the wrong one can be called, with the wrong number of arguments, and that normally crashes R. Writing R Extensions explains that PACKAGE confines the search and speeds it up, and the help page of .Call recommends it or a native symbol object for anything called often. The manual’s timing section measured the difference as small but real for functions called millions of times (Writing R Extensions: Registering native routines).

Errors from the lookup

When the name cannot be found, R says so in a message that is the same on every platform. These are the real texts, captured by tryCatch() (the container’s directory is replaced by <dir> so that the script, not the page, hides the path). The last three lines show the same failure for .C(), .Fortran() and .External(); only .Fortran() says "Fortran symbol name".

dyn.load(paste0("add", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
message_of <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) {
    gsub(getwd(), "<dir>", conditionMessage(e), fixed = TRUE)
  })
}

# A symbol that is not in any loaded shared object.
message_of(.Call("nope"))
#> [1] "C symbol name \"nope\" not in load table"

# A symbol searched in the wrong shared object, or in one that is not loaded.
message_of(.Call("nope", PACKAGE = "add"))
#> [1] "\"nope\" not available for .Call() for package \"add\""
message_of(.Call("add", 1, 2, PACKAGE = "nosuchdll"))
#> [1] "\"add\" not available for .Call() for package \"nosuchdll\""

# A file that does not exist (the second line is the operating system's text).
message_of(dyn.load("missing.so"))
#> [1] "unable to load shared object '<dir>/missing.so':\n  <dir>/missing.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory"

# The same symbol name on the other three interfaces.
message_of(.C("nope"))
#> [1] "C symbol name \"nope\" not in load table"
message_of(.Fortran("nope"))
#> [1] "Fortran symbol name \"nope\" not in load table"
message_of(.External("nope"))
#> [1] "C symbol name \"nope\" not in load table"

Source: R documentation: .Call

The second line of the dyn.load() message is the operating system’s own text (this one is glibc’s), so it differs on macOS and Windows. All four lookup errors have the same remedy: check the spelling, check that the shared object was built from the current source and loaded, and check that the function is not static and, in C++, is declared extern "C".

Handling R objects in C

What a SEXP is

Every R object that C code touches is a SEXP, a pointer to a structure the headers call SEXPREC. Think of it as a variant type: the same pointer type refers to a numeric vector, a list, a function, an environment, a call or NULL, and TYPEOF(x) returns a code that says which. C code must therefore check the type before it uses the data, and it gets at the data through accessor functions, never by looking inside the structure (the structure is not part of the API and its layout is allowed to change). The types that package code meets most often are these.

TYPEOF() code R object How C reads or builds it

REALSXP

numeric (double) vector

double *REAL(x) or the read-only const double *REAL_RO(x); Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, n)

INTSXP

integer vector (also the codes of a factor)

int *INTEGER(x), INTEGER_RO(x); missing value NA_INTEGER

LGLSXP

logical vector

int *LOGICAL(x), LOGICAL_RO(x); values 0, 1 or NA_LOGICAL

CPLXSXP and RAWSXP

complex and raw vectors

COMPLEX(x) (an Rcomplex has members r and i), RAW(x)

STRSXP

character vector

STRING_ELT(x, i) gives a CHARSXP; CHAR() of that gives a const char *; SET_STRING_ELT() stores one

VECSXP

list (generic vector)

VECTOR_ELT(x, i), SET_VECTOR_ELT(x, i, v)

NILSXP

NULL

the constant R_NilValue

LISTSXP, LANGSXP

pairlist, call

CAR, CDR, TAG; see .External() and the callback example below

CLOSXP, ENVSXP, SYMSXP

function, environment, name

Rf_isFunction(), Rf_eval(), Rf_install()

Source: Writing R Extensions: Details of R types

Two types in that table deserve a remark. A CHARSXP is not an R-level object but the immutable, shared element of a character vector: R keeps one copy of each distinct string in a global cache, so C code must never modify the bytes behind CHAR(). And LISTSXP is the old Lisp-style pairlist; an R list is a VECSXP, which is why the test for an R list is Rf_isNewList() and not Rf_isList() (Writing R Extensions: Handling lists). R Internals describes all the types, including the ones that are not for packages (R Internals: SEXPs).

The Rf_ prefix and R_NO_REMAP

The functions in the manual’s examples carry an Rf_ prefix (Rf_allocVector, Rf_error, Rf_ScalarReal), and so do all the examples on this page. R’s headers also define short names for many of them (allocVector, error, length), which are macros that expand to the prefixed names, and those short names clash easily with system headers and other libraries. Defining R_NO_REMAP before any R header removes the macros and leaves only the prefixed names. The manual states the facts that matter: the prefix is optional in C code and recommended for new C code; since R 4.5.0 R_NO_REMAP is always defined when the R headers are included from C++, so C++ code must use the Rf_ names; and a package that defines it itself should guard it with #ifndef R_NO_REMAP to avoid compiler warnings about redefinition (Writing R Extensions: The R API).

The NEWS entries behind that: R 4.4.0 added the environment variable _R_CXX_USE_NO_REMAP_, which makes R CMD INSTALL (and so R CMD check) compile C++ code with -DR_NO_REMAP, and said that this was planned to become the default; R 4.5.0 made it the default and revised the manual to describe the remapped entry points (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.4.0 and 4.5.0). usethis::use_c() writes a template that starts with #define R_NO_REMAP, as the shelf example later shows. Two related switches exist for other headers: R_NO_REMAP_RMATH does the same for Rmath.h (the distribution functions), and STRICT_R_HEADERS, which removes the old S-compatibility definitions (PI, Calloc, Realloc, Free and the DOUBLE_* constants), has been the default since R 4.5.0, with R_Calloc, R_Realloc, R_Free and M_PI as the replacements.

A vector in, a vector out

The next file has three functions that show the pattern every .Call() routine follows: check or coerce the arguments, allocate the result, fill it through a pointer, copy the attributes that should survive, and return. overdue_days() requires a double vector and returns the days beyond the loan limit element by element; is_late() coerces to integers and returns a logical vector; count_late() calls is_late() and counts.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* Days beyond the loan period, element by element; NA and NaN pass through. */
SEXP overdue_days(SEXP days, SEXP limit) {
  if (!Rf_isReal(days)) {
    Rf_error("'days' must be a double vector");
  }
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(days);
  double lim = Rf_asReal(limit);
  const double *d = REAL_RO(days);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, n));
  double *o = REAL(out);
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (ISNAN(d[i])) {
      o[i] = d[i];
    } else {
      o[i] = d[i] > lim ? d[i] - lim : 0.0;
    }
  }
  SEXP nms = Rf_getAttrib(days, R_NamesSymbol);
  if (nms != R_NilValue) {
    Rf_setAttrib(out, R_NamesSymbol, nms);
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return out;
}

/* TRUE when a loan is late, NA when the number of days is missing. */
SEXP is_late(SEXP days, SEXP limit) {
  SEXP d = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(days, INTSXP));
  int lim = Rf_asInteger(limit);
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(d);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(LGLSXP, n));
  const int *pd = INTEGER_RO(d);
  int *po = LOGICAL(out);
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    po[i] = pd[i] == NA_INTEGER ? NA_LOGICAL : pd[i] > lim;
  }
  UNPROTECT(2);
  return out;
}

/* How many loans are late; missing values are not counted. */
SEXP count_late(SEXP days, SEXP limit) {
  SEXP flags = PROTECT(is_late(days, limit));
  const int *p = LOGICAL_RO(flags);
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(flags);
  int total = 0;
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (p[i] != NA_LOGICAL && p[i]) {
      total++;
    }
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return Rf_ScalarInteger(total);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Handling R objects in C

Several points in the file are worth a line each.

  • XLENGTH() and R_xlen_t are for lengths. R vectors can be longer than 2^31 - 1 elements on 64-bit platforms (the length is a signed 64-bit integer, with a practical limit of 52 bits), and LENGTH() and Rf_length() return an int that cannot hold such lengths; code that loops with an int index works until the day someone passes a very long vector (R Internals: Long vectors).

  • REAL_RO() returns a const pointer. The vector accessors have read-only variants (INTEGER_RO, LOGICAL_RO, DATAPTR_RO), and for a character vector or a list only read-only access exists, because writing straight into those would break the memory manager’s assumptions. The manual adds that these pointers are valid only for vectors of positive length: a zero-length vector has no data, so memcpy() of zero elements through such a pointer is undefined behaviour unless the length is checked first (Writing R Extensions: Vector accessor functions). top_days() below guards its copy for this reason.

  • REAL(x) is a function call, not a field access. Store the pointer in a variable before the loop, as the file does, instead of calling REAL(x)[i] on every iteration.

  • The result is allocated with Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, n). Unlike numeric(n) in R, Rf_allocVector() does not initialise the elements of an atomic vector (it only does so for lists and character vectors), so every element must be written before the object is returned.

  • The names are copied explicitly, with Rf_getAttrib() and Rf_setAttrib(). Attributes are not copied automatically; a function that should keep names, dim or class has to do it.

  • PROTECT() and UNPROTECT() bracket the lifetime of the new object; the section after next explains why.

The script builds the R wrappers, calls the functions on a vector of loan durations that contains a missing value (NA) and a not-a-number (NaN), and shows what the type check does. storage.mode<- in the wrapper converts to double while keeping the names, which as.double() would drop.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB vectors.c`; the loan durations are typed in.
dyn.load(paste0("vectors", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
overdue_days <- function(days, limit = 21) {
  storage.mode(days) <- "double"
  .Call("overdue_days", days, limit, PACKAGE = "vectors")
}
is_late <- function(days, limit = 21L) {
  .Call("is_late", days, limit, PACKAGE = "vectors")
}
count_late <- function(days, limit = 21L) {
  .Call("count_late", days, limit, PACKAGE = "vectors")
}

days <- c(
  loan1 = 14, loan2 = 35, loan3 = NA, loan4 = 21, loan5 = 28.5, loan6 = NaN
)
overdue_days(days)
#> loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4 loan5 loan6
#>   0.0  14.0    NA   0.0   7.5   NaN
overdue_days(days, limit = 14)
#> loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4 loan5 loan6
#>   0.0  21.0    NA   7.0  14.5   NaN
overdue_days(numeric())
#> numeric(0)

# Names survive; NA and NaN are told apart.
is.na(overdue_days(days))
#> loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4 loan5 loan6
#> FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
is.nan(overdue_days(days))
#> loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4 loan5 loan6
#> FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

# The C code coerces, so integers and doubles both work (28.5 is cut to 28).
is_late(days)
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE    NA FALSE  TRUE    NA
count_late(days)
#> [1] 2
count_late(c(30L, 10L, NA, 22L))
#> [1] 2
typeof(count_late(days))
#> [1] "integer"

# A wrong type is an error raised from C.
tryCatch(
  .Call("overdue_days", "14", 21, PACKAGE = "vectors"),
  error = conditionMessage
)
#> [1] "'days' must be a double vector"

Source: R documentation: mode and storage.mode

overdue_days() passes both NA and NaN through unchanged because it copies the element when ISNAN() is true. That is a deliberate choice: the next table shows that C distinguishes the two only with ISNA(), and it is easy to turn every NaN into NA by writing NA_REAL where the input should have been kept.

Missing values in C

R’s missing values are values of the C types, and each type has its own constant and its own test.

Type Missing value Test

double

NA_REAL (a particular NaN bit pattern)

ISNA(x) is true for NA only; ISNAN(x) is true for NA and NaN; R_FINITE(x) is false for NA, NaN, Inf and -Inf; R_IsNaN(x) is true for NaN only. Never compare with ==.

int (integer)

NA_INTEGER (the smallest int)

x == NA_INTEGER

int (logical)

NA_LOGICAL

x == NA_LOGICAL; any other non-zero value is TRUE

SEXP (character element)

NA_STRING

STRING_ELT(x, i) == NA_STRING (pointer comparison; the string is "NA" to CHAR())

Source: Writing R Extensions: Missing and IEEE special values

The manual adds that these tests apply to doubles only, that isfinite() should not be used in place of R_FINITE(), and that Inf and -Inf are tested by comparing with R_PosInf and R_NegInf. .Call() passes missing values straight into the C code; it is .C() that refuses them unless NAOK = TRUE, as a later section shows.

Character vectors

A character vector is a STRSXP: a vector whose elements are CHARSXP nodes. Reading goes through STRING_ELT() and CHAR(); writing builds a CHARSXP with Rf_mkChar() (from a NUL-terminated C string), Rf_mkCharLen() (from part of a buffer) or Rf_mkCharLenCE() (with an encoding mark) and stores it with SET_STRING_ELT(). Rf_mkString() makes a whole length-one character vector from a C string, and Rf_ScalarString() from a CHARSXP. The function below keeps the first blank-delimited word of each string, passes NA through, and, because it copies the bytes of an element it did not interpret, copies the encoding mark of the original with it.

#include <string.h>
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* The first blank-delimited word of each string; NA stays NA. */
SEXP first_word(SEXP x) {
  if (!Rf_isString(x)) {
    Rf_error("'x' must be a character vector");
  }
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(x);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(STRSXP, n));
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    SEXP el = STRING_ELT(x, i);
    if (el == NA_STRING) {
      SET_STRING_ELT(out, i, NA_STRING);
      continue;
    }
    const char *s = CHAR(el);
    int len = (int) strcspn(s, " \t");
    SET_STRING_ELT(out, i, Rf_mkCharLenCE(s, len, Rf_getCharCE(el)));
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return out;
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Handling character data

The encoding rules are the part of this that goes wrong in practice. A CHARSXP can be marked as UTF-8 or Latin-1, and the bytes behind CHAR() are in whatever encoding the mark says. When C code needs to interpret the characters, the manual recommends Rf_translateChar() (to the current locale’s encoding) or Rf_translateCharUTF8() (to UTF-8, which almost always represents the string faithfully), because both handle any input and allocate with R_alloc(); and when it only moves a string unchanged, as here, it should keep the mark with Rf_getCharCE() and Rf_mkCharLenCE() (Writing R Extensions: Character encoding issues). The help page of .C() adds a reason to prefer .Call() for text: a missing string reaches .C() code as the text "NA", which cannot be told from a real "NA".

Lists, classes and matrices

Lists, classes and dimensions are all attributes and vectors of vectors. loan_stats() below builds a named list with Rf_mkNamed() (which takes a C array of names ended by an empty string), fills its three elements with SET_VECTOR_ELT(), and sets the class attribute with Rf_classgets(). day_gaps() allocates a matrix with Rf_allocMatrix() (column-major, like R) and sets dimnames to a two-element list, reusing the names of the input for both dimensions. A data frame is a list of equal-length columns with names, row.names and class attributes; it is simplest to build the columns in C and call as.data.frame() or data.frame() in the R wrapper (Rcpp, later, does it in one expression).

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* A classed, named list: count, mean and maximum of the non-missing days. */
SEXP loan_stats(SEXP days) {
  SEXP d = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(days, REALSXP));
  const double *p = REAL_RO(d);
  R_xlen_t len = XLENGTH(d);
  int n = 0;
  double sum = 0.0, max = R_NegInf;
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    if (ISNAN(p[i])) {
      continue;
    }
    n++;
    sum += p[i];
    if (p[i] > max) {
      max = p[i];
    }
  }
  const char *names[] = {"n", "mean", "max", ""};
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_mkNamed(VECSXP, names));
  SET_VECTOR_ELT(out, 0, Rf_ScalarInteger(n));
  SET_VECTOR_ELT(out, 1, Rf_ScalarReal(n > 0 ? sum / n : NA_REAL));
  SET_VECTOR_ELT(out, 2, Rf_ScalarReal(n > 0 ? max : NA_REAL));
  SEXP cls = PROTECT(Rf_mkString("loan_stats"));
  Rf_classgets(out, cls);
  UNPROTECT(3);
  return out;
}

/* A matrix of differences x[i] - x[j], with names(x) as both dimnames. */
SEXP day_gaps(SEXP x) {
  SEXP xr = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(x, REALSXP));
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(xr);
  const double *p = REAL_RO(xr);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocMatrix(REALSXP, (int) n, (int) n));
  double *o = REAL(out);
  for (R_xlen_t j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      o[i + n * j] = p[i] - p[j];
    }
  }
  SEXP nms = Rf_getAttrib(x, R_NamesSymbol);
  if (nms != R_NilValue) {
    SEXP dn = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, 2));
    SET_VECTOR_ELT(dn, 0, nms);
    SET_VECTOR_ELT(dn, 1, nms);
    Rf_setAttrib(out, R_DimNamesSymbol, dn);
    UNPROTECT(1);
  }
  UNPROTECT(2);
  return out;
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Attributes

Both functions follow the protection rule: every object that is created and then kept while something else is allocated is protected, and the count of UNPROTECT() matches. In loan_stats() the three scalars are not protected separately because they are handed to SET_VECTOR_ELT() immediately, and the list that now owns them is protected. The manual explains this: protecting an object protects everything it points to, so the elements of a protected list are protected. In day_gaps() the dimnames list is protected with its own PROTECT() and released with an UNPROTECT(1) as soon as it has been attached.

One script exercises both strings.c and structures.c. It feeds first_word() an ASCII vector with an NA and an empty string, then an accented name written as a UTF-8 string literal: the result is still marked UTF-8. It then prints the list from loan_stats() and gives the class a print method in R, and finally shows the dimnames of the matrix.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB strings.c` and `R CMD SHLIB structures.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("strings", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
dyn.load(paste0("structures", .Platform$dynlib.ext))

authors <- c("Ursula K. Le Guin", "Iris  Fenwick", NA, "Mara Quill", "")
.Call("first_word", authors, PACKAGE = "strings")
#> [1] "Ursula" "Iris"   NA       "Mara"   ""

# Encoding is kept: a UTF-8 string stays marked as UTF-8.
x <- "André Pinto"
Encoding(.Call("first_word", x, PACKAGE = "strings"))
#> [1] "UTF-8"
.Call("first_word", x, PACKAGE = "strings")
#> [1] "André"

days <- c(loan1 = 14, loan2 = 35, loan3 = NA, loan4 = 21)
stats <- .Call("loan_stats", days, PACKAGE = "structures")
class(stats)
#> [1] "loan_stats"
names(stats)
#> [1] "n"    "mean" "max"
unclass(stats)
#> $n
#> [1] 3
#>
#> $mean
#> [1] 23.33333
#>
#> $max
#> [1] 35
#>
print.loan_stats <- function(x, ...) {
  cat(sprintf("%d loans, mean %.1f days, longest %g\n", x$n, x$mean, x$max))
  invisible(x)
}
stats
#> 3 loans, mean 23.3 days, longest 35

# A matrix with dimnames set from C.
.Call("day_gaps", days, PACKAGE = "structures")
#>       loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4
#> loan1     0   -21    NA    -7
#> loan2    21     0    NA    14
#> loan3    NA    NA    NA    NA
#> loan4     7   -14    NA     0
dim(.Call("day_gaps", c(1, 2, 3), PACKAGE = "structures"))
#> [1] 3 3

Source: Writing R Extensions: Classes

Errors, warnings, output and interrupts

C code reports problems to R with Rf_error() and Rf_warning(), which take a printf-style format and have the same effect as stop() and warning() in R code. Output goes through Rprintf() (R’s standard output, which a GUI console, sink() or a parallel worker may redirect) and REprintf() (R’s error stream), never printf() to the C library’s stdout, whose text may not appear in the console at all; writing complete lines is advised. A long loop should call R_CheckUserInterrupt() now and then, because no part of R can be interrupted while it runs compiled code otherwise.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <R_ext/Utils.h>

/* Stops on a negative value, warns about a missing one. */
SEXP checked_sqrt(SEXP x) {
  double v = Rf_asReal(x);
  if (ISNAN(v)) {
    Rf_warning("missing value, returning NA");
    return Rf_ScalarReal(NA_REAL);
  }
  if (v < 0) {
    Rf_error("'x' must be non-negative, not %g", v);
  }
  return Rf_ScalarReal(sqrt(v));
}

/* Prints a summary on standard output and a note on standard error. */
SEXP report(SEXP days) {
  SEXP d = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(days, REALSXP));
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(d);
  Rprintf("%lld loans\n", (long long) n);
  REprintf("(note: written to the error stream)\n");
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return R_NilValue;
}

/* A long loop that can be interrupted from the console. */
SEXP busy(SEXP iterations) {
  double steps = Rf_asReal(iterations);
  double acc = 0.0;
  for (double i = 0; i < steps; i++) {
    if (((long long) i) % 1000000 == 0) {
      R_CheckUserInterrupt();
    }
    acc += 1.0;
  }
  return Rf_ScalarReal(acc);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Error signaling

There are rules to follow in these functions. Rf_error() never returns: R implements it as a non-local jump (a longjmp) to the nearest tryCatch() or the top level, skipping the C code between, so nothing after the call runs: memory from R_alloc() is reclaimed by R on an error, memory from R_Calloc() is not, and R restores the protect stack by itself. The format string is a template, so a message that comes from data must go through "%s" (Rf_error("%s", msg)), or a % in it will be interpreted. Rf_errorcall(call, ...) and Rf_warningcall(call, ...) take the call to blame, and R_NilValue omits it. The script shows what R makes of them. The error is an ordinary simpleError whose call is that of the R function that called .Call(); capture.output() sees the Rprintf() line, and its type = "message" form sees the REprintf() line.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB conditions.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("conditions", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
checked_sqrt <- function(x) .Call("checked_sqrt", x, PACKAGE = "conditions")

checked_sqrt(2)
#> [1] 1.414214

# Rf_error() becomes an ordinary R error, blamed on the calling R function.
err <- tryCatch(checked_sqrt(-4), error = identity)
conditionMessage(err)
#> [1] "'x' must be non-negative, not -4"
class(err)
#> [1] "simpleError" "error"       "condition"
deparse(conditionCall(err))
#> [1] "checked_sqrt(-4)"

# Rf_warning() becomes an ordinary R warning.
warn <- tryCatch(checked_sqrt(NA), warning = identity)
conditionMessage(warn)
#> [1] "missing value, returning NA"
class(warn)
#> [1] "simpleWarning" "warning"       "condition"

# Rprintf() goes through R's output connection and REprintf() through its
# error connection, so each can be captured on its own.
report <- function(days) {
  invisible(.Call("report", days, PACKAGE = "conditions"))
}
msg <- capture.output(
  out <- capture.output(report(c(14, 21, 35))),
  type = "message"
)
out
#> [1] "3 loans"
msg
#> [1] "(note: written to the error stream)"

# R_CheckUserInterrupt() lets Ctrl-C stop a long loop; without one, it cannot be
# stopped. This run is short enough to finish.
busy <- function(n) .Call("busy", n, PACKAGE = "conditions")
busy(5e6)
#> [1] 5e+06

Source: R documentation: capture.output

The call shown in deparse(conditionCall(err)) is checked_sqrt(-4), the wrapper, which is what a user of the function wants in the message; the unwrapped .Call("checked_sqrt", x, PACKAGE = "conditions") would not help them. The last lines run busy(), the loop with R_CheckUserInterrupt(); it finishes here because nobody presses Ctrl-C. The manual gives a version for Fortran, rchkusr(), and adds that the code behind many API entry points can itself be interrupted or raise an error, so any C code that holds a resource should be written with that in mind (Writing R Extensions: Allowing interrupts).

When the resource is a file, a lock, or a buffer from R_Calloc(), the tools for a clean exit are in the manual’s section on condition handling and cleanup code: R_UnwindProtect() runs a cleanup function on both normal return and non-local jumps, R_ExecWithCleanup() is the older and simpler form, and R_tryCatch() and R_tryEval() catch conditions (Writing R Extensions: Condition handling and cleanup code). An alternative that avoids the problem is to keep the allocation in R: allocate the buffer in R (numeric(n)) and pass it in.

Calling R from C

C code can call back into R. The routine below receives a function f, a vector and an environment, and applies the function to each element with Rf_lang2() (which builds the call f(arg)) and Rf_eval(). Each intermediate object is protected, and the check of the result’s type is made in C, since the function could return anything. The environment rho is passed from R as environment() because the API has no supported entry point for the current environment (the manual’s table of replacements tells packages to call environment() in R and pass the result).

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* Call the R function f on each element of x and collect the numbers. */
SEXP map_dbl(SEXP f, SEXP x, SEXP rho) {
  if (!Rf_isFunction(f)) {
    Rf_error("'f' must be a function");
  }
  SEXP xr = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(x, REALSXP));
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(xr);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, n));
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    SEXP arg = PROTECT(Rf_ScalarReal(REAL(xr)[i]));
    SEXP call = PROTECT(Rf_lang2(f, arg));
    SEXP res = PROTECT(Rf_eval(call, rho));
    if (!Rf_isNumeric(res) || XLENGTH(res) != 1) {
      Rf_error("'f' must return a single number");
    }
    REAL(out)[i] = Rf_asReal(res);
    UNPROTECT(3);
  }
  UNPROTECT(2);
  return out;
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Evaluating R expressions from C

An error inside f is an ordinary R error: it unwinds through the C function and arrives at the caller’s tryCatch(), so the message is the one that f raised. The two checks in the C code give the other two messages.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB callback.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("callback", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
map_dbl <- function(f, x) {
  .Call("map_dbl", f, x, environment(), PACKAGE = "callback")
}

late_fee <- function(days) pmax(days - 21, 0) * 0.25
map_dbl(late_fee, c(14, 21, 35, 49))
#> [1] 0.0 0.0 3.5 7.0
map_dbl(\(d) d / 7, 1:3)
#> [1] 0.1428571 0.2857143 0.4285714

# Errors raised by the R function pass through the C code to the caller.
tryCatch(map_dbl(\(d) stop("boom at ", d), 1:3), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "boom at 1"
tryCatch(map_dbl(\(d) c(d, d), 1:3), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "'f' must return a single number"
tryCatch(map_dbl("late_fee", 1:3), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "'f' must be a function"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Evaluating R expressions from C

A callback costs as much as an R function call, so a loop that calls R on every element gives back most of what the C code saved. Callbacks are for the occasional call (an objective function in an optimiser, a user hook) rather than for the inner loop.

The rules that keep a .Call routine safe

The manual’s rules for .Call() and .External() code can be written as a short list.

  • Treat the arguments as read-only. .Call() and .External() do not copy their arguments, so a vector that C code modifies in place changes every R variable that shares it. R shares freely (y <- x copies nothing, as Assignment, Names and Values shows). Copy with Rf_duplicate() (or Rf_shallow_duplicate() when only the top level changes) before modifying, and see Memory and Copy Semantics for how R decides when a copy is needed. The macros NAMED and SET_NAMED that older books use were replaced by reference counting in R 4.0.0; package code should use MAYBE_SHARED(), MAYBE_REFERENCED(), NO_REFERENCES() and MARK_NOT_MUTABLE(), which are documented in the section on named objects and copying (Writing R Extensions: Named objects and copying).

  • Check the types. A wrong guess gives a segmentation fault, not an R error. Test with TYPEOF() or Rf_isReal() and friends, or coerce with Rf_coerceVector() (which allocates, so the result is protected) or the scalar readers Rf_asReal(), Rf_asInteger() and Rf_asLogical(), which ignore all but the first element, as the add() example showed. Rf_asRboolean() (R 4.5.0) is the stricter version that errors on a length other than one. Coercion in C does not dispatch on class (a factor is just an integer), so it is usually better to coerce in the R wrapper.

  • Allocate with R and protect what you allocate (next section), and never keep a SEXP in a global C variable across calls unless it is registered with R_PreserveObject().

  • Stay on the main thread. The manual is explicit that the R API may be called only from the main thread of the R process; using it from another thread can corrupt memory.

  • Prefer the documented API. The last section of the page is about which entry points are documented.

PROTECT and UNPROTECT

Why objects need protecting

R frees the memory of objects automatically, by garbage collection, and it can run the collector whenever it allocates anything. An object that C code has just created and holds only in a local variable is invisible to the collector: nothing in R’s own data structures refers to it, so the next allocation can free it, and the pointer in the C variable then points at memory that may be reused. The result is not an error but corrupt output or a crash, often much later and somewhere else. PROTECT() puts the object on a stack that the collector treats as a root, and UNPROTECT(n) pops the last n entries. Writing R Extensions states the rule precisely: it is the object that is protected, not the pointer variable, so assigning a different object to p after PROTECT(p) leaves the new object unprotected (Writing R Extensions: Handling the effects of garbage collection).

The protect stack has rules, and the manual lists four of them for functions that cooperate.

  • Balance. PROTECT and UNPROTECT calls must balance in each function, and a function may unprotect only what it protected itself. A jump out of the function (an error, an interrupt) restores the stack automatically.

  • Callers protect arguments. The caller keeps every argument protected for the whole call, which is why .Call() routines do not protect their arguments.

  • Return values are unprotected. An object returned by a function must be protected at once by the caller, even if the callee only returned something that already existed, because it may have been duplicated.

  • Everything allocates. Assume that any API function or macro may allocate and so may trigger a collection; the code that is safe today because a function happens not to allocate can fail after a change in R.

The simplest style follows from them: SEXP x = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(...)); on creation, one UNPROTECT(n) before every return, with n the number of objects protected in that function. The stack has a fixed size (10,000 entries by default), so a loop must not protect something new on every iteration without releasing it, and the better design is to store objects in a protected container (a list) or to unprotect them immediately after use. callback.c above does exactly that: it protects three objects inside the loop and UNPROTECT(3) at the end of each iteration. Anything allocated and handed straight to SET_VECTOR_ELT() or SET_STRING_ELT() is safe from then on, as loan_stats() shows.

Changing a protected value: PROTECT_WITH_INDEX

The rule that the object is protected, and not the pointer, means that code that replaces a protected object (by coercing, duplicating or growing it) must protect the replacement. When the old object is no longer needed, PROTECT_WITH_INDEX(s, &ipx) records the stack position and REPROTECT(s, ipx) stores a new object in that position, so the stack does not grow. total_days() below coerces an integer argument to double only if it needs to, and keeps whichever object it ends up using protected under one index.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* Bug: one PROTECT too many, so the protect stack is one entry deeper. */
SEXP leaky(SEXP x) {
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, 1));
  REAL(out)[0] = Rf_asReal(x) * 2.0;
  return out;
}

/* Bug: one UNPROTECT too many, so the caller's entry is dropped. */
SEXP too_many(SEXP x) {
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, 1));
  REAL(out)[0] = Rf_asReal(x) * 2.0;
  UNPROTECT(2);
  return out;
}

/* Correct: the coerced copy replaces the protected value in place. */
SEXP total_days(SEXP x) {
  PROTECT_INDEX ipx;
  SEXP v = x;
  PROTECT_WITH_INDEX(v, &ipx);
  if (TYPEOF(v) != REALSXP) {
    REPROTECT(v = Rf_coerceVector(v, REALSXP), ipx);
  }
  double total = 0.0;
  const double *p = REAL_RO(v);
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < XLENGTH(v); i++) {
    total += p[i];
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return Rf_ScalarReal(total);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Handling the effects of garbage collection

The file also contains the two classic mistakes, in functions that compile without a warning and return the right number: leaky() has one PROTECT() too many (it forgot UNPROTECT(1)), and too_many() has one UNPROTECT() too many. .Call() checks the protect stack when a routine returns, and when the count has changed it prints a warning. The text of that warning is real; the two numbers are the size of the protect stack before and after the call, so they depend on how deeply R is nested at that moment, and the values below are the ones from a top-level Rscript run. A leak makes the second number larger, an excess UNPROTECT() makes it smaller. The messages are written directly to the error stream when the routine returns, before the value is printed, so they are not conditions: tryCatch(..., warning = ) and withCallingHandlers() do not see them (in this test the handler did not run). The wrong routines still return 2.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB protect.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("protect", .Platform$dynlib.ext))

# Correct code: PROTECT_WITH_INDEX and REPROTECT keep the coerced copy alive.
total_days <- function(x) .Call("total_days", x, PACKAGE = "protect")
total_days(c(14, 21, 35))
#> [1] 70
total_days(1:4)
#> [1] 10

# Unbalanced code still returns its value; the protect stack is what is wrong.
# R notices when the .Call returns and prints a warning on the console. The two
# numbers in it are the stack sizes before and after, and they vary from run to
# run (they depend on how deeply R is nested at that moment).
.Call("leaky", 1, PACKAGE = "protect")
#> Warning: stack imbalance in '.Call', 2 then 3
#> [1] 2
.Call("too_many", 1, PACKAGE = "protect")
#> Warning: stack imbalance in '.Call', 2 then 1
#> [1] 2

Source: Writing R Extensions: Handling the effects of garbage collection

The messages catch only a mismatch in the count. A missing PROTECT() is silent until the collector runs at the wrong moment, and that is much harder to find. R has two tools for it. gctorture(TRUE) makes the collector run on nearly every allocation, so an unprotected object is freed at once and the crash happens close to its cause; R CMD check --use-gct runs a package’s examples, tests and vignettes that way (R documentation: gctorture). A build of R configured with --enable-strict-barrier also marks freed nodes, so touching one raises an error that names the old type. The sections on checking memory access in Writing R Extensions describe these, Valgrind and the address sanitizer (Writing R Extensions: Checking memory access).

R_PreserveObject and the other ways to keep an object alive

PROTECT() is for the duration of one call. An object that has to survive between calls (a cache, a handle returned to R as an external pointer) is kept alive with R_PreserveObject(x) and released with R_ReleaseObject(x); the manual calls this less efficient than normal protection and to be used sparingly, because releasing it is then the author’s responsibility, usually from a finalizer. For parsers there is a multi-set interface (R_NewPreciousMSet, R_PreserveInMSet, R_ReleaseFromMSet), and the old UNPROTECT_PTR() is dangerous to mix with UNPROTECT() and is not for new code. External pointers, which wrap a C pointer in an R object with a finalizer, are the way to return a C data structure to R, and have their own section (Writing R Extensions: External pointers and weak references).

Memory allocation: R_alloc and R_Calloc

C code needs memory that is not an R object: a scratch buffer, a working copy. R provides two families, and the difference is who cleans up (Writing R Extensions: Memory allocation).

Function Lifetime Use it for

R_alloc(n, size)

Until the .C(), .Call() or .External() call returns, or vmaxset() releases it; freed on an error or interrupt.

Scratch space inside one call. Preferred, because no error path can leak it. Aligned for double only; R_allocLD() is aligned for long double.

R_Calloc(n, type), R_Realloc(p, n, type), R_Free(p)

Until R_Free(). A wrapper over malloc that signals an R error if allocation fails.

Memory that outlives one call, or too large to hold for the whole call. The caller must free it on every path, including errors and interrupts (often with on.exit() in the R wrapper).

S_alloc()

As R_alloc, zero-filled.

Avoid for large sizes: its length argument is a long, which is too small on 64-bit Windows.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Memory allocation

memory.c shows both. median_days() copies the non-missing values into an R_alloc() buffer, sorts it with R_rsort() (R’s own sort for doubles) and reads the middle; top_days() sorts a copy held in an R_Calloc() buffer and frees it with R_Free() before returning. A check on the length precedes the Memcpy(), for the reason given above about zero-length vectors. Memory from R_Calloc() does not necessarily come from the same pool as malloc(), so it must not be passed to free() or strdup().

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <R_ext/Utils.h>

/* Median of the non-missing days: scratch space from R_alloc. */
SEXP median_days(SEXP days) {
  SEXP d = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(days, REALSXP));
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(d);
  const double *p = REAL_RO(d);
  double *buf = (double *) R_alloc((size_t) n, sizeof(double));
  R_xlen_t m = 0;
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (!ISNAN(p[i])) {
      buf[m++] = p[i];
    }
  }
  double med = NA_REAL;
  if (m > 0) {
    R_rsort(buf, (int) m);
    med = (m % 2 == 1) ? buf[m / 2] : 0.5 * (buf[m / 2 - 1] + buf[m / 2]);
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return Rf_ScalarReal(med);
}

/* The k largest values, in decreasing order: a buffer from R_Calloc. */
SEXP top_days(SEXP days, SEXP k) {
  SEXP d = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(days, REALSXP));
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(d);
  int kk = Rf_asInteger(k);
  if (kk == NA_INTEGER || kk < 0) {
    Rf_error("'k' must be a non-negative integer");
  }
  if (kk > n) {
    kk = (int) n;
  }
  double *buf = R_Calloc((size_t) n, double);
  if (n > 0) {
    Memcpy(buf, REAL_RO(d), (size_t) n);
  }
  R_rsort(buf, (int) n);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, kk));
  for (int i = 0; i < kk; i++) {
    REAL(out)[i] = buf[n - 1 - i];
  }
  R_Free(buf);
  UNPROTECT(2);
  return out;
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: User-controlled memory

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB memory.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("memory", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
median_days <- function(days) .Call("median_days", days, PACKAGE = "memory")
top_days <- function(days, k) {
  .Call("top_days", days, as.integer(k), PACKAGE = "memory")
}

days <- c(14, 35, NA, 21, 28, 7, 49)
median_days(days)
#> [1] 24.5
median(days, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 24.5
median_days(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
#> [1] NA
median_days(1:4)
#> [1] 2.5

top_days(days, 3)
#> [1] NA 49 35
top_days(c(5, 1, 3), 10)
#> [1] 5 3 1
tryCatch(top_days(days, -1), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "'k' must be a non-negative integer"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Transient storage allocation

The macros were named Calloc, Realloc and Free in older code. The prefixed forms were introduced in R 3.4.0 and are preferred; the unprefixed ones, with the old constant PI, were removed from the headers in R 4.5.0 when strict R headers became the default (the manual says so, and the NEWS entry names them as the legacy definitions that went). R_Calloc and its relatives expand to calls to R_chk_calloc, R_chk_realloc and R_chk_free, which the manual says not to call directly. The next file is old code of exactly that kind.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
SEXP f(SEXP x) {
  double *buf = Calloc(10, double);
  Free(buf);
  return Rf_ScalarReal(PI);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: User-controlled memory

On R 4.6.1 it does not compile. This is the compiler’s complaint (filtered to the lines that matter), and the build’s exit status, 1.

R CMD SHLIB old_macros.c 2>&1 | grep -E ": (warning|error):"
#> old_macros.c:4:17: warning: implicit declaration of function ‘Calloc’; did you mean ‘calloc’? [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
#> old_macros.c:4:28: error: expected expression before ‘double’
#> old_macros.c:5:3: warning: implicit declaration of function ‘Free’; did you mean ‘free’? [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
#> old_macros.c:6:24: error: ‘PI’ undeclared (first use in this function)

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 4.5.0

The fix is the prefix: R_Calloc(10, double), R_Free(buf) and M_PI.

Registering native routines

The ISBN check as a .Call routine

So far every routine was found by its name, by searching the symbols of the shared object. The rest of the page uses one routine as its running example: the ISBN-13 check of the shelf package. It takes a character vector and returns a logical vector. Its rule is the one is_valid_isbn13() implements in R: keep the digits, reject an X, require exactly 13 digits, and require that the digits multiplied alternately by 1 and 3 add up to a multiple of 10. NA and the empty string are FALSE. The file has a header with the prototype, and starts with #define R_NO_REMAP, so every R function in it carries the Rf_ prefix. The constant ISBN_DIGITS has a default and can be overridden from the compiler command line, which the src/Makevars section uses.

#define R_NO_REMAP
#include <ctype.h>
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include "isbn.h"

#ifndef ISBN_DIGITS
#define ISBN_DIGITS 13
#endif

/* One string: keep the digits, reject an X, weight 1 and 3 alternately. */
static int valid_isbn(const char *s) {
  int n = 0, sum = 0;
  for (; *s != '\0'; s++) {
    if (isdigit((unsigned char) *s)) {
      if (n == ISBN_DIGITS) {
        return 0;
      }
      sum += (*s - '0') * (n % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 3);
      n++;
    } else if (*s == 'X' || *s == 'x') {
      return 0;
    }
  }
  return n == ISBN_DIGITS && sum % 10 == 0;
}

/* Vectorised: FALSE for NA, for the empty string and for a wrong check digit. */
SEXP isbn13_valid(SEXP x) {
  if (!Rf_isString(x)) {
    Rf_error("'x' must be a character vector");
  }
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(x);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(LGLSXP, n));
  int *po = LOGICAL(out);
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    SEXP el = STRING_ELT(x, i);
    po[i] = el != NA_STRING && valid_isbn(CHAR(el));
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return out;
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Handling R objects in C

#ifndef SHELF_ISBN_H
#define SHELF_ISBN_H

#include <Rinternals.h>

SEXP isbn13_valid(SEXP x);

#endif

Source: Writing R Extensions: Registering native routines

Built with R CMD SHLIB isbn.c and loaded as before, the routine agrees with the R version on a vector that contains valid ISBNs in hyphenated and bare forms, one with a wrong check digit, the empty string, NA, a ten-digit ISBN-10 and a string with an X. The comparison function is the R version from the shelf package, copied into the script because the script runs in the directory of the compiled objects.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB isbn.c`; the ISBN strings are typed in.
dyn.load(paste0("isbn", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
isbn13_c <- function(x) .Call("isbn13_valid", as.character(x), PACKAGE = "isbn")

# The same rule in R, for comparison.
isbn13_r <- function(x) {
  digits <- gsub("[^0-9X]", "", toupper(x))
  ok <- !is.na(digits) & nchar(digits) == 13L &
    !grepl("X", digits, fixed = TRUE)
  vapply(seq_along(digits), \(i) {
    if (!ok[[i]]) {
      return(FALSE)
    }
    d <- as.integer(strsplit(digits[[i]], "")[[1L]])
    sum(d * rep(c(1L, 3L), length.out = 13L)) %% 10L == 0L
  }, logical(1L))
}

isbns <- c(
  "978-0-306-40615-7", "9780001000100", "978-0-01-100112-9",
  "", NA, "978-0-00-200029-1", "0-306-40615-2", "978-0-00-X00029-1"
)
isbn13_c(isbns)
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE
identical(isbn13_c(isbns), isbn13_r(isbns))
#> [1] TRUE
isbn13_c(character())
#> logical(0)
tryCatch(isbn13_c(9780306406157), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] TRUE
tryCatch(
  .Call("isbn13_valid", 9780306406157, PACKAGE = "isbn"),
  error = conditionMessage
)
#> [1] "'x' must be a character vector"

Source: R documentation: .Call

R_registerRoutines and R_init_<name>

Registration replaces the search by a table that the shared object builds when it is loaded. When R loads foo.so, it looks for a function named R_init_foo and calls it with a DllInfo pointer; when it unloads the object, it calls R_unload_foo if there is one. The name is made from the file name without its extension, so it must be a valid part of a C identifier: the manual advises ASCII letters, digits and underscores only. The initialiser calls R_registerRoutines() with five arguments: the DllInfo, and one NULL-terminated array for each interface, in the order .C(), .Call(), .Fortran(), .External(). The array element types are R_CMethodDef, R_CallMethodDef, R_FortranMethodDef and R_ExternalMethodDef. Each entry holds the name by which R refers to the routine, a function pointer cast to DL_FUNC, and the number of arguments; .External() routines use -1 for "any number". The entries for .C() and .Fortran() may add an array of argument types (REALSXP, INTSXP, LGLSXP, STRSXP, VECSXP, SINGLESXP) that R checks on every call.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <R_ext/Rdynload.h>
#include "isbn.h"

static const R_CallMethodDef call_methods[] = {
  {"isbn13_valid", (DL_FUNC) &isbn13_valid, 1},
  {NULL, NULL, 0}
};

void R_init_shelf(DllInfo *dll) {
  R_registerRoutines(dll, NULL, call_methods, NULL, NULL);
  R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE);
  R_forceSymbols(dll, TRUE);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Registering native routines

Two more calls close the loophole of finding things by string. R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE) says that the shared object is not to be searched for symbols not in the table, so .Call("name") finds only registered names. R_forceSymbols(dll, TRUE) says that foreign function calls into this object must name the entry point with an R object (a native symbol object), and not with a character string at all. The manual’s example uses a package mypkg with a registered routine reg and an unregistered unreg: without registration both .Call("reg") and .Call("unreg") work; with R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE) only the first does; with useDynLib(mypkg, .registration = TRUE, .fixes = "C_") in NAMESPACE, .Call(C_reg) works too; and with R_forceSymbols(dll, TRUE) only .Call(C_reg) works. That last arrangement is what a package normally wants: all its own calls go directly to its own code, and nobody finds its entry points by accident. A user who needs one from outside, for debugging, can write .Call(mypkg:::C_reg).

The next script builds this object as shelf.so (R CMD SHLIB -o shelf.so isbn.c init.c; the file name makes R_init_shelf() the initialiser), loads it next to the unregistered isbn.so, and shows the registered routine as an R object, the call by object, the call by string on the unregistered object, and what the two registered-only settings do to the string calls and to a wrong number of arguments. The object returned by getDLLRegisteredRoutines() lists the table; routines$.Call$isbn13_valid is a native symbol object.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB isbn.c` and `R CMD SHLIB -o shelf.so isbn.c init.c`.
# The file name decides which initialiser R looks for: shelf.so runs
# R_init_shelf(), while isbn.so has none and registers nothing.
dyn.load(paste0("isbn", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
dyn.load(paste0("shelf", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
isbns <- c("978-0-306-40615-7", "978-0-01-100112-9", NA)

# What the initialiser registered.
routines <- getDLLRegisteredRoutines("shelf")
class(routines)
#> [1] "DLLRegisteredRoutines"
names(routines)
#> [1] ".C"        ".Call"     ".Fortran"  ".External"
routines$.Call
#>              numParameters
#> isbn13_valid             1

# A registered routine is an R object with a name, an address and an arity.
info <- routines$.Call$isbn13_valid
class(info)
#> [1] "CallRoutine"      "NativeSymbolInfo"
names(info)
#> [1] "name"          "address"       "dll"           "numParameters"
info$name
#> [1] "isbn13_valid"
info$numParameters
#> [1] 1

# Calling through the object skips the lookup by name.
.Call(info, isbns)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE

# Without registration a string finds any exported symbol in the shared object.
.Call("isbn13_valid", isbns, PACKAGE = "isbn")
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE

# R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE) and R_forceSymbols(dll, TRUE): only objects.
message_of <- function(expr) tryCatch(expr, error = conditionMessage)
message_of(.Call("isbn13_valid", isbns, PACKAGE = "shelf"))
#> [1] "\"isbn13_valid\" not available for .Call() for package \"shelf\""
message_of(.Call("valid_isbn", isbns, PACKAGE = "shelf"))
#> [1] "\"valid_isbn\" not available for .Call() for package \"shelf\""

# The registered arity is checked on every call.
message_of(.Call(info, isbns, isbns))
#> [1] "Incorrect number of arguments (2), expecting 1 for 'isbn13_valid'"
message_of(.Call(info))
#> [1] "Incorrect number of arguments (0), expecting 1 for 'isbn13_valid'"

Source: R documentation: getDLLRegisteredRoutines

Both error messages are R’s. The string call to the forced object says that the name is not available "for package shelf", although the routine exists, because the object refuses string lookups; and a wrong number of arguments is an error that names the routine and both counts, instead of undefined behaviour in C.

The skeleton generator

tools::package_native_routine_registration_skeleton() writes the init.c for you. It reads the R code of a package for .C(), .Call(), .Fortran() and .External() calls, takes the routine names and the number of arguments from the calls, and prints C source with the FIXME comment that reminds you to check the declarations against the C code. NEWS for R 3.4.0 says it automated registration for over 90% of the CRAN packages that lacked it, and that many of its failures were real bugs in the packages: dozens called entry points with varying numbers of arguments or entry points that were not there. The script builds a throwaway package whose R code still calls .Call("isbn13_valid", x, PACKAGE = "shelf") and runs the tool on it.

# A throwaway package whose R code still calls the C routine by name.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "shelf")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(
  c(
    "is_valid_isbn13_c <- function(x) {",
    '  .Call("isbn13_valid", x, PACKAGE = "shelf")',
    "}"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "R", "isbn-c.R")
)
writeLines(
  c("export(is_valid_isbn13_c)", "useDynLib(shelf)"),
  file.path(pkg, "NAMESPACE")
)
writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: shelf", "Version: 0.1.0", "Title: Skeleton",
    "Description: Skeleton.", "License: MIT"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")
)

# The tool reads the R code and prints a registration skeleton to the console.
tools::package_native_routine_registration_skeleton(pkg)
#> #include <R.h>
#> #include <Rinternals.h>
#> #include <stdlib.h> // for NULL
#> #include <R_ext/Rdynload.h>
#>
#> /* FIXME:
#>    Check these declarations against the C/Fortran source code.
#> */
#>
#> /* .Call calls */
#> extern SEXP isbn13_valid(SEXP);
#>
#> static const R_CallMethodDef CallEntries[] = {
#>     {"isbn13_valid", (DL_FUNC) &isbn13_valid, 1},
#>     {NULL, NULL, 0}
#> };
#>
#> void R_init_shelf(DllInfo *dll)
#> {
#>     R_registerRoutines(dll, NULL, CallEntries, NULL, NULL);
#>     R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE);
#> }
unlink(pkg, recursive = TRUE)

Source: R documentation: package_native_routine_registration_skeleton

The output is the starting point, not the end: the prototype extern SEXP isbn13_valid(SEXP); is guessed from the call and belongs in a header (as isbn.h here), the argument counts have to be checked, and R_forceSymbols() is not added. The manual’s walk-through of converting the splines package lists the remaining steps: add useDynLib(pkg, .registration = TRUE) to NAMESPACE; change .Call("name", ..., PACKAGE = "pkg") calls to .Call(name, ...) with the R object; add R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE) and then R_forceSymbols(dll, TRUE); and consider hiding the C functions from the symbol table (Writing R Extensions: Example: converting a package to use registration). Hiding is done with attribute_hidden on each function, or with PKG_CFLAGS = $(C_VISIBILITY) in src/Makevars together with attribute_visible on R_init_pkg alone (Writing R Extensions: Controlling visibility); it removes any chance of a name clash and speeds up loading slightly. Fortran entry points cannot use attribute_hidden; the variable F_VISIBILITY does the job for them.

useDynLib in NAMESPACE

The NAMESPACE file loads the shared object and, with .registration = TRUE, creates in the package’s namespace one R variable for each registered routine. The directive has more forms, all from the manual.

NAMESPACE directive Effect

useDynLib(shelf)

Loads shelf.so when the namespace is loaded. Calls still use PACKAGE = "shelf" and strings.

useDynLib(shelf, .registration = TRUE)

Loads the object and defines an R variable for every registered routine, named as registered (isbn13_valid), so code can say .Call(isbn13_valid, x).

useDynLib(shelf, .registration = TRUE, .fixes = "C_")

As above with a prefix: the variable is C_isbn13_valid. stats uses this, which is why its code reads .C(C_pansari, ...). KernSmooth uses .fixes = "F_" for Fortran.

useDynLib(shelf, isbn13_valid) or useDynLib(shelf, sym = isbn13_valid)

Looks up the listed symbols once, at load time, and defines variables for them (optionally renamed). Superseded by registration.

dll = useDynLib(shelf)

Also assigns the DLL object to the variable dll, so .Call(dll$isbn13_valid, x) looks the symbol up at each call.

Source: Writing R Extensions: useDynLib

The manual adds a caution: using .registration or .fixes for a package that does not register its routines only slows loading, and once routines are registered, the new R variables must not be exported by accident by an exportPattern() in NAMESPACE. With roxygen2 the directive is written in the R sources as @useDynLib shelf, .registration = TRUE (and the same for the .fixes argument), usually in the package-level help file, and devtools::document() copies it into NAMESPACE. The next section does exactly that, and usethis::use_c() and usethis::use_rcpp() print the lines to paste.

R also checks all of this. R CMD check tests every foreign function call for a PACKAGE argument, or a way to deduce the DLL, and tools::checkFF() reports the cases that need attention (R documentation: checkFF). Since R 3.4.0, R CMD check --as-cran notes a package that neither registers its routines nor declares what it does about symbol search. The environment variable _R_CHECK_NATIVE_ROUTINE_REGISTRATION_ makes R CMD check report packages whose DLL lacks the registration entry points (it needs the nm utility on the PATH, and objdump on Windows); the section on tools in R Internals documents it (R Internals: Tools). The real report is shown in the section on the C API, from a package that fails it.

Compiled code in a package: the shelf example

A package that contains compiled code has a src/ directory. R CMD INSTALL builds it with the same R CMD SHLIB machinery as above: when src/ has sources with a known extension, or a Makevars file, and no Makefile, it reads Makevars first, then R’s system makefile, then the user’s personal Makevars, compiles every source file in src/ and links them into shelf.so (or shelf.dll). The shared object is installed in the libs/ directory of the installed package, and useDynLib in NAMESPACE loads it with the namespace. A src/Makefile, if present, replaces this mechanism; the manual says a Makevars is better and a Makefile should be needed only exceptionally (Writing R Extensions: Creating shared objects). Package structure in general is the subject of Creating Packages, namespaces of Packages, Libraries and Namespaces, and documentation and roxygen2 of Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes.

The shelf package of those pages has an R function is_valid_isbn13(). This section adds a C version, is_valid_isbn13_c(), to a copy of the package: the files isbn.c, isbn.h and init.c shown above, a two-line src/Makevars, an R wrapper, and the useDynLib directive. The Rcpp version of the same function is a second copy, later. Paths in the transcripts are shortened to ~/shelf.

Creating src/ with usethis

usethis::use_c() creates src/, a .gitignore inside it that keeps the compiled .o, .so and .dll files out of version control, and a template source file. It prints the lines to paste into the package-level R file. Both in this transcript and below, the path is shortened.

> usethis::use_c("isbn")
✔ Setting active project to "~/shelf".
✔ Creating 'src/'.
✔ Adding "*.o", "*.so", and "*.dll" to 'src/.gitignore'.
☐ Copy and paste the following lines into 'R/shelf-package.R':
  ## usethis namespace: start
  #' @useDynLib shelf, .registration = TRUE
  ## usethis namespace: end
  NULL
✔ Writing 'src/isbn.c'.
☐ Edit 'src/isbn.c'.

Source: usethis package documentation: use_c

The template src/isbn.c has three lines (#define R_NO_REMAP, #include <R.h> and #include <Rinternals.h>); it was replaced by the isbn.c shown earlier. The R file named in the message holds the roxygen tag, and a second file has the wrapper. The wrapper coerces with as.character() in R, where a factor is converted properly, and passes the registered symbol object to .Call(); because NAMESPACE has .registration = TRUE, the variable isbn13_valid exists in the namespace.

## usethis namespace: start
#' @useDynLib shelf, .registration = TRUE
## usethis namespace: end
NULL

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Managing imports and exports

#' Check ISBN-13 strings with compiled code
#'
#' `is_valid_isbn13_c()` gives the same answers as [is_valid_isbn13()], but the
#' check runs in C through the `.Call()` interface (`src/isbn.c`).
#'
#' @param x A character vector of ISBNs; `NA` and empty strings are allowed.
#' @returns A logical vector of the same length as `x`, `FALSE` for `NA` and for
#'   the empty string.
#' @examples
#' is_valid_isbn13_c(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "978-0-01-100112-9", NA))
#' @export
is_valid_isbn13_c <- function(x) {
  .Call(isbn13_valid, as.character(x))
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Calling .Call

devtools::document() and load_all()

devtools::document() runs roxygen2, which loads the package first, so it compiles src/. pkgload::load_all() (called by devtools::load_all()) compiles src/ with pkgbuild::compile_dll() when a source file is newer than the object, and loads the result with the R code, which is the edit-compile-test loop of package development. It builds with debugging flags (-UNDEBUG -Wall -pedantic -g -O0), so compiler warnings appear while you work, and the transcript below shows them quiet because the code compiles cleanly. Two details are visible in the output: the -DISBN_DIGITS=13 that comes from src/Makevars, and that Writing 'NAMESPACE' appears twice, once before the package is compiled and loaded and once after. The compiler lines are shortened, the first line that names the compiler is omitted, and so is the line that prints the temporary library the package is installed into.

> devtools::document()
ℹ Updating shelf documentation
Writing 'NAMESPACE'
ℹ Loading shelf
ℹ Re-compiling shelf (debug build)
── R CMD INSTALL ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
* installing *source* package ‘shelf’ ...
** this is package ‘shelf’ version ‘0.1.0’
** using staged installation
** libs
gcc -std=gnu2x -I"<R_HOME>/include" -DISBN_DIGITS=13 -fPIC -UNDEBUG -Wall -pedantic -g -O0 -c init.c -o init.o
gcc -std=gnu2x -I"<R_HOME>/include" -DISBN_DIGITS=13 -fPIC -UNDEBUG -Wall -pedantic -g -O0 -c isbn.c -o isbn.o
gcc -std=gnu2x -shared -o shelf.so init.o isbn.o -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR
** checking absolute paths in shared objects and dynamic libraries
* DONE (shelf)
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
Writing 'NAMESPACE'
Writing 'is_valid_isbn13_c.Rd'

Source: devtools package documentation: document

The generated NAMESPACE gains two lines, the export of the new function and the useDynLib() directive; the rest is the file of the earlier pages.

# Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand

S3method(format,book)
S3method(print,book)
S3method(print,summary.book)
S3method(summary,book)
export(book)
export(clean_books)
export(clean_loans)
export(is_valid_isbn13)
export(is_valid_isbn13_c)
export(loan_summary)
export(loans_per_month)
export(new_book)
export(normalise_isbn)
export(overdue_loans)
export(validate_book)
useDynLib(shelf, .registration = TRUE)

Source: Writing R Extensions: useDynLib

One practical trap is worth knowing. make knows which .c file produced which .o file, but not which headers a file includes. If only isbn.h changes, nothing is rebuilt, and the second R CMD INSTALL of an unchanged tree says so, with this real line in place of the compiler lines:

** libs
make: Nothing to be done for 'all'.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Creating shared objects

Delete the .o and .so files in src/ (or use R CMD INSTALL --preclean, or pkgbuild::clean_dll()) after changing a header, a Makevars file or the compiler flags. R CMD build cleans src/ itself when it makes the tarball (the build prints * cleaning src), which is why compiled objects never belong in a source package.

R CMD INSTALL
