The command a user types is R CMD INSTALL shelf in the directory that contains the package. It compiles src/ with R’s own flags (not the debug flags of load_all()), installs, and tests that the installed package loads. The transcript keeps the lines that concern the compiled code, shortens the compiler lines as before, and marks the omitted ones with [...]; the container’s temporary paths in the other lines are dropped.

R CMD INSTALL shelf
#> * installing *source* package ‘shelf’ ...
#> ** this is package ‘shelf’ version ‘0.1.0’
#> ** using staged installation
#> ** libs
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -I"<R_HOME>/include" -DISBN_DIGITS=13 -fPIC -O2 -c init.c -o init.o
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -I"<R_HOME>/include" -DISBN_DIGITS=13 -fPIC -O2 -c isbn.c -o isbn.o
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -shared -o shelf.so init.o isbn.o -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR
#> ** R
#> ** data
#> [...]
#> ** testing if installed package can be loaded from temporary location
#> ** checking absolute paths in shared objects and dynamic libraries
#> ** testing if installed package can be loaded from final location
#> ** testing if installed package keeps a record of temporary installation path
#> * DONE (shelf)

Source: R documentation: INSTALL

With the package installed, the script loads it and checks the compiled function against the R one on the books data set of the package, and looks at what registration created: the routine in the registration table with its arity, the R variable isbn13_valid in the namespace, and the loaded DLL.

# The shelf copy with src/isbn.c installed by `R CMD INSTALL shelf`.
library(shelf)
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days

is_valid_isbn13_c(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "978-0-01-100112-9", NA, ""))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE
identical(is_valid_isbn13_c(books$isbn), is_valid_isbn13(books$isbn))
#> [1] TRUE
sum(is_valid_isbn13_c(books$isbn))
#> [1] 14

# The registration table is part of the namespace.
getDLLRegisteredRoutines("shelf")$.Call$isbn13_valid$numParameters
#> [1] 1
ns <- asNamespace("shelf")
class(get("isbn13_valid", envir = ns))
#> [1] "CallRoutine"      "NativeSymbolInfo"
dll <- getLoadedDLLs()[["shelf"]]
class(dll)
#> [1] "DLLInfo"
basename(dll[["path"]])
#> [1] "shelf.so"

# The R function calls the symbol object, never a string.
body(is_valid_isbn13_c)
#> {
#>     .Call(isbn13_valid, as.character(x))
#> }

# tools::checkFF() inspects foreign function calls; no output means no findings.
tools::checkFF(package = "shelf")

Source: R documentation: getLoadedDLLs

The compiled function and the R function return the same logical vector on the sixteen ISBNs of the data set, of which fourteen are valid. tools::checkFF() found nothing to report.

R CMD check

R CMD check has several checks for compiled code. The transcript is the relevant part of R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual --no-tests --ignore-vignettes on the built tarball, with the remote CRAN-incoming checks off and the header that names the platform removed. Every line shown is OK. The checks that did not appear are those about the quick options used here (vignettes and tests were skipped, so this is not the full check of the earlier pages).

* checking whether package ‘shelf’ can be installed ... OK
* checking foreign function calls ... OK
* checking line endings in C/C++/Fortran sources/headers ... OK
* checking line endings in Makefiles ... OK
* checking compilation flags in Makevars ... OK
* checking for GNU extensions in Makefiles ... OK
* checking for portable use of $(BLAS_LIBS) and $(LAPACK_LIBS) ... OK
* checking use of PKG_*FLAGS in Makefiles ... OK
* checking use of SHLIB_OPENMP_*FLAGS in Makefiles ... OK
* checking pragmas in C/C++ headers and code ... OK
* checking compiled code ... OK

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking and building packages

Two of those lines concern files you write for compiled code: "checking compilation flags in Makevars" (the check that rejects -Wall and friends in PKG_CFLAGS, shown to fail in the section on src/Makevars) and "checking compiled code" (the check of the API usage, shown to fail in the section on the C API). The container’s R was built with distribution flags, so the full check also reported a NOTE that the compilation used non-portable flags such as -Wformat; it comes from how this R was built, not from the package, and is not shown.

src/Makevars and the compiler flags

src/Makevars is a makefile fragment that R CMD SHLIB includes before R’s own Makeconf. It is the place for settings that the package needs, and it is not the place for settings that belong to the person or the machine that builds it. The manual lists the variables.

Variable Use

PKG_CPPFLAGS

Preprocessor options for C and C++ files: -I include paths, -D and -U definitions, -include, -pthread. Include paths belong here and not in PKG_CFLAGS or PKG_CXXFLAGS: there a platform include path can take precedence, which has caused hard-to-debug failures.

PKG_CFLAGS, PKG_CXXFLAGS, PKG_FFLAGS, PKG_FCFLAGS

Extra compiler flags for C, C++, fixed-form Fortran and free-form Fortran. PKG_FCFLAGS exists for the rare package that needs different flags for the two Fortran forms.

PKG_LIBS

Linker options: -L and -l for libraries the code uses. Macros from R’s Makeconf are available for numerical code: LAPACK_LIBS, BLAS_LIBS and FLIBS, which must appear in that order; FLIBS is added automatically when the package has Fortran sources.

CXX_STD

The C++ standard: CXX17, CXX20, CXX23 or CXX26 (not a make directive: no quotes, no trailing comment). For C there is no variable; the standard is set in SystemRequirements as USE_C17 or USE_C23 for a package that depends on R (>= 4.3.0).

OBJECTS

The list of object files to build, when the package does not want every source in src/ (for example to include files from subdirectories). If Makevars sets it, R CMD SHLIB does not.

C_VISIBILITY, CXX_VISIBILITY, F_VISIBILITY

Macros from R’s Makeconf that hold the compiler’s flag for hiding symbols; used as PKG_CFLAGS = $(C_VISIBILITY).

SHLIB_OPENMP_CFLAGS, SHLIB_OPENMP_CXXFLAGS, SHLIB_OPENMP_FFLAGS

The OpenMP flags for the compiler R was built with; see below.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using Makevars

src/Makevars is read on Linux and macOS; on Windows Makevars.win is read instead, and since R 4.2.0 Makevars.ucrt is preferred to Makevars.win when both exist (NEWS for R 4.2.0, which also added Makefile.ucrt, configure.ucrt and cleanup.ucrt). A configure script that writes Makevars from Makevars.in is the next step when the package has to adapt to the system. The Makevars of the shelf package is two lines, a comment and a definition. PKG_CPPFLAGS = -DISBN_DIGITS=13 is a preprocessor option and so belongs in that variable; it passes the digit count to isbn.c, which has #ifndef ISBN_DIGITS to supply a default when the file is compiled alone.

# Preprocessor definitions belong in PKG_CPPFLAGS, not in the compiler flags.
PKG_CPPFLAGS = -DISBN_DIGITS=13

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using Makevars

Why a package must not set -Wall

The manual says in so many words not to put compiler-specific diagnostic flags in a distributed Makevars: -O2, -Wall, -pedantic and every other -W flag are specific to GCC and compilers that copy its options (for Oracle’s compilers, -W flags passed arguments to compiler phases). Variables such as CPPFLAGS and CFLAGS themselves must not be set at all, because users and sites set them. R CMD check enforces this. This is the real output of R CMD check --as-cran on a deliberately wrong tiny package (probe, shown in the section on the C API) whose src/Makevars is the single line PKG_CFLAGS = -Wall -O3:

* checking compilation flags in Makevars ... WARNING
Non-portable flags in variable 'PKG_CFLAGS':
  -Wall -O3

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using Makevars

The right place for warnings is the developer’s own Makevars file. The manual encourages package developers to enable a reasonable amount of compiler diagnostics this way, for example -Wall -pedantic for GCC and LLVM. The personal file is ~/.R/Makevars (or ~/.R/Makevars-<platform>, or Makevars.win on Windows), or any file named by the environment variable R_MAKEVARS_USER; there is also a site-wide Makevars.site and R_MAKEVARS_SITE; the R FAQ answers the question of changing flags in one short entry that points to the same manual section (R FAQ 8.4: How can I change compilation flags?). The file used for every example on this page (its path given with R_MAKEVARS_USER for the test run) is:

CFLAGS = -O0 -Wall -pedantic
CXXFLAGS = -O0 -Wall -pedantic
FFLAGS = -O0 -Wall -pedantic
FCFLAGS = -O0 -Wall -pedantic

Source: R Installation and Administration: Customizing package compilation

It sets the flags for all four compilers (the variables are CFLAGS, CXXFLAGS, FFLAGS and FCFLAGS) and switches off optimisation so that the compiler’s analysis is simple. When the C standard or C++ standard is non-default the matching variable (C17FLAGS, CXX20FLAGS, and so on) must be set instead. The effect is easy to see on a file that is sloppy in the way -Wall catches:

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

SEXP double_it(SEXP x) {
  int unused = 0;
  return Rf_ScalarReal(2.0 * Rf_asReal(x));
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using Makevars

R_MAKEVARS_USER=user-makevars R CMD SHLIB --preclean sloppy.c
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -I"<R_HOME>/include" -fPIC -O0 -Wall -pedantic -c sloppy.c -o sloppy.o
#> sloppy.c: In function ‘double_it’:
#> sloppy.c:5:7: warning: unused variable ‘unused’ [-Wunused-variable]
#>     5 |   int unused = 0;
#>       |       ^~~~~~
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -shared -o sloppy.so sloppy.o -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR

Source: R Installation and Administration: Customizing package compilation

The -Wextra flag is stricter than -Wall and is worth trying, with one known exception: the idiom (DL_FUNC) &name in a registration table converts a function pointer to another function pointer type, and -Wextra (through -Wcast-function-type) reports it on each entry. That is why the file above uses -Wall -pedantic. All the C, C++ and Fortran files in this page were built with these flags and produced no warning.

The C++ standard: CXX_STD

R compiles package C++ code with a standard that depends on the R version, and the manual’s advice is to say which standard the code needs. The NEWS entries are: R 4.3.0 changed the default to C++17 where available (C++14 or C++11 otherwise); the manual says that from R 4.4.0 only a C++17 compiler is selected as the default; R 4.6.0 changed the default to C++20 where available, and otherwise C++17, and C++11 and C++14 are no longer supported; and packages can request C++17 if they need it. Newer standards (C++23, C++26) can be requested as the compiler allows. The request is made in two places that must agree: CXX_STD = CXX17 in src/Makevars (and Makevars.win, Makevars.ucrt), and SystemRequirements: C++17 in DESCRIPTION; if they differ, SystemRequirements wins, and R CMD check checks that they match. Code that wants a feature of a newer standard should test for it, with the standard’s feature-test macros, rather than assume it.

The next pair of runs makes this visible. std.cpp returns the value of __cplusplus that its compiler saw, and a constant that comes from the command line.

#define R_NO_REMAP
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

#ifndef LOAN_DAYS
#define LOAN_DAYS 21
#endif

/* The language standard the compiler was asked for, as 201703 or 202002. */
extern "C" SEXP cpp_standard() {
  return Rf_ScalarInteger((int) __cplusplus);
}

/* A value injected from the command line by -DLOAN_DAYS=... */
extern "C" SEXP loan_days_default() {
  return Rf_ScalarInteger(LOAN_DAYS);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using C++ code

CXX_STD = CXX17
PKG_CPPFLAGS = -DLOAN_DAYS=28

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using Makevars

Built in a directory with no Makevars, the compiler uses R’s default; built in a directory with the file above, R CMD SHLIB honours CXX_STD and PKG_CPPFLAGS. The compile line of the second build is

R CMD SHLIB std.cpp
#> specified C++17
#> using C++17
#> g++ -std=gnu++17 -I"<R_HOME>/include" -DLOAN_DAYS=28 -fPIC -O2 -c std.cpp -o std.o
#> g++ -std=gnu++17 -shared -o std.so std.o -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using C++ code

(without the line that names the compiler and the system, and with the flags shortened as before; specified C++17 and using C++17 are R’s own lines, and the -DLOAN_DAYS=28 comes from PKG_CPPFLAGS). The script loads whichever std.so is in the current directory and asks it. Run in the directory that was built without a Makevars, it prints the lines shown after the code.

# std.cpp is built twice: by `R CMD SHLIB std.cpp` in one directory, and again
# in a directory with a Makevars file that sets CXX_STD and PKG_CPPFLAGS. Run
# this script from either directory, after building there.
dyn.load(paste0("std", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
c(
  standard = .Call("cpp_standard", PACKAGE = "std"),
  loan_days = .Call("loan_days_default", PACKAGE = "std")
)
#>  standard loan_days
#>    202002        21

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using C++ code

Run in the directory that has the Makevars (the previous script, saved as check-standard.R one directory up), it reports the standard and the constant that the file asked for:

cd with-makevars
Rscript ../check-standard.R
#>  standard loan_days
#>    201703        28

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using C++ code

The numbers are the values of __cplusplus: 202002 is C++20 (the R 4.6 default) and 201703 is C++17. For a package that has src/Makefile instead of Makevars, the manual shows how to take the compiler from R CMD config CXX20 and its relatives; a configure script must do the same, and must not hard-code g++.

C standards, and the Fortran and OpenMP variables

For C, R 4.5.0 made the configure script choose a compiler option that selects C23 when one is available (gcc 15 defaults to C23 on its own). The effect on package code is stricter C: bool, true and false are keywords, K&R-style declarations are gone, and an empty parameter list now means no parameters, so code that relied on an unprototyped declaration can stop compiling. A package that cannot move can ask for an older standard with USE_C17 (or USE_C99, USE_C90) in SystemRequirements, and a user can force one when installing with R CMD INSTALL --use-C17; the same option exists for R CMD SHLIB, as its help shows. The __STDC_VERSION__ macro tells which standard the compiler claims (202311L for C23; some compilers used 202000L for a draft), but the manual advises testing for the feature the code needs and not the version (Writing R Extensions: C standards). The Fortran side has its own page in this section, and the Fortran Reference covers the language.

OpenMP is the usual way to use several threads inside compiled code. The compiler flag differs between compilers, so a package takes it from R: it puts $(SHLIB_OPENMP_CFLAGS) in both PKG_CFLAGS and PKG_LIBS for C code (and SHLIB_OPENMP_CXXFLAGS and SHLIB_OPENMP_FFLAGS for the other two languages, with a different recipe for Fortran), guards OpenMP-specific code with #ifdef _OPENMP, and includes the macros only when the code really uses OpenMP. Some toolchains, Apple’s clang among them, have no OpenMP support at all, and a note in the manual says that the C++ macro applies to the default C++ compiler and not necessarily to the one selected for C++17 or C++20, for which a configure check is advised. Writing -fopenmp directly into PKG_CXXFLAGS works with gcc and fails elsewhere, which is why R CMD check has a check named "checking use of SHLIB_OPENMP_*FLAGS in Makefiles" (it appears in the transcript of the earlier section). Calling the R API from threaded code is, in the manual’s words, for experts only and strongly discouraged: the R API changes internal data structures, and errors must be signalled only from the main thread. The threading model of R’s parallel packages is the subject of Parallel and Asynchronous Computing; the manual’s section is OpenMP support.

.C: plain pointers

How .C passes arguments

.C() is the traditional interface and the simplest to write for: the C function takes pointers to plain C data and returns void. R copies each argument, passes a pointer to the copy, and returns a list of the (possibly modified) copies, with the names that were given to the arguments. No R header is needed, and the C function does not have to know it is called from R. The mapping from R storage modes to C types is fixed.

R storage mode C type Fortran type

integer, logical

int *

integer

double (numeric)

double * (or float * with the Csingle attribute, set by as.single())

double precision (or real)

complex

Rcomplex *, a structure with members r and i

double complex

character

char **

one string only, as character*255; deprecated

raw

unsigned char *

not allowed

list, other

SEXP * or SEXP (read-only; use .Call() instead)

not allowed

Source: R documentation: .C

A logical is sent as 0, 1 or INT_MIN (the last only when NAOK = TRUE), and the code should return one of the three values. The C type for an R integer is int, which is 32 bits on every platform R runs on, and not long: code ported from S-PLUS that used long * is wrong on most 64-bit platforms (Writing R Extensions: Interface functions .C and .Fortran). Strings need most care. On entry the contents of a character vector are copied to a char ** array; the C code can shorten a string by writing a '\0', but it cannot lengthen one, and a missing string arrives as the text "NA". For anything that is not plain numbers, use .Call().

A .C routine

The convolution of two sequences, the manual’s own example, makes the routine. convolve() takes the two sequences and their lengths as pointers and fills a result array that the caller allocated, since a C function cannot return a vector through .C(); the R wrapper allocates it with double(length(a) + length(b) - 1) and names it so that $ab extracts it from the returned list. The file also registers a second name, convolve_checked, for the same function with its argument types, which is how the type check below is made.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <R_ext/Rdynload.h>

/* .C passes pointers to copies of the arguments and returns them as a list. */
void convolve(double *a, int *na, double *b, int *nb, double *ab) {
  int nab = *na + *nb - 1;
  for (int i = 0; i < nab; i++) {
    ab[i] = 0.0;
  }
  for (int i = 0; i < *na; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < *nb; j++) {
      ab[i + j] += a[i] * b[j];
    }
  }
}

/* The same routine under a second name, registered with argument types. */
static R_NativePrimitiveArgType convolve_types[] = {
  REALSXP, INTSXP, REALSXP, INTSXP, REALSXP
};

static const R_CMethodDef c_methods[] = {
  {"convolve_checked", (DL_FUNC) &convolve, 5, convolve_types},
  {NULL, NULL, 0, NULL}
};

void R_init_convolve(DllInfo *dll) {
  R_registerRoutines(dll, c_methods, NULL, NULL, NULL);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Interface functions .C and .Fortran

The script shows the list that .C() returns, the refusal of missing values, the effect of a type mistake on an unregistered routine, the registered version of the check, and the old DUP argument. A few results need explaining.

  • DUP and ENCODING are accepted for old code and ignored. Before R 3.2.0 DUP = FALSE avoided the copy; since that version the NEWS says it is ignored and that the arguments are duplicated as DUP = TRUE would do, and the help page says .Call() is much preferred. The script shows that adding DUP = FALSE changes nothing.

  • A NA, NaN or Inf in an argument is an error: NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 1). NAOK = TRUE turns the check off, and the values then reach the C code as they are; the result 1 NA shows that NA * 1 is NA.

  • A mistake in the type is not an error at all. Passing the double 3 where the C code reads an int * makes the C code see the bit pattern of a double, whose low four bytes are zero on a little-endian machine, so na is 0 and the result is 0 0 0 0 instead of 0 1 2 3, with no message. The same mistake with a character string for a double * would read pointer values as numbers. The manual says as much: coerce every argument to the right mode before calling (as.double(), as.integer()).

  • Registering the argument types gives the check: wrong type for argument 2 in call to convolve_checked for the double, and Incorrect number of arguments (4), expecting 5 for 'convolve_checked' for the missing one, naming the routine and both counts. A mismatch between the number of types in the array and the number of arguments cannot be checked by the compiler, so count them.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB convolve.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("convolve", .Platform$dynlib.ext))

# .C copies every argument, passes pointers, and returns them as a list.
convolve <- function(a, b) {
  .C("convolve",
    as.double(a), as.integer(length(a)),
    as.double(b), as.integer(length(b)),
    ab = double(length(a) + length(b) - 1),
    PACKAGE = "convolve"
  )$ab
}
convolve(c(1, 2, 3), c(0, 1, 0.5))
#> [1] 0.0 1.0 2.5 4.0 1.5
res <- .C("convolve", c(1, 2), 2L, c(3, 4), 2L, ab = double(3),
  PACKAGE = "convolve"
)
str(res)
#> List of 5
#>  $   : num [1:2] 1 2
#>  $   : int 2
#>  $   : num [1:2] 3 4
#>  $   : int 2
#>  $ ab: num [1:3] 3 10 8

# DUP and ENCODING are accepted for old code and ignored: arguments are copied.
args <- list("convolve", c(1, 2), 2L, c(3, 4), 2L, ab = double(3))
identical(
  do.call(.C, c(args, DUP = FALSE, PACKAGE = "convolve")),
  do.call(.C, c(args, PACKAGE = "convolve"))
)
#> [1] TRUE

# Missing and non-finite values are refused unless NAOK = TRUE.
message_of <- function(expr) tryCatch(expr, error = conditionMessage)
message_of(convolve(c(1, NA, 3), 1))
#> [1] "NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 1)"
.C("convolve", c(1, NA), 2L, 1, 1L, ab = double(2),
  NAOK = TRUE, PACKAGE = "convolve"
)$ab
#> [1]  1 NA

# Nothing checks the types of an unregistered routine. A double where C reads
# an int (here na = 3) is not an error; on a little-endian machine the low
# four bytes of 3.0 are zero, so C sees na = 0 and the answer is wrong.
.C("convolve", c(1, 2, 3), 3, c(0, 1), 2L, ab = double(4),
  PACKAGE = "convolve"
)$ab
#> [1] 0 0 0 0

# The registered copy of the routine knows its types and its arity.
message_of(.C("convolve_checked", c(1, 2, 3), 3, c(0, 1), 2L, ab = double(4)))
#> [1] "wrong type for argument 2 in call to convolve_checked"
message_of(.C("convolve_checked", c(1, 2, 3), 3L, c(0, 1), 2L))
#> [1] "Incorrect number of arguments (4), expecting 5 for 'convolve_checked'"
.C("convolve_checked", c(1, 2, 3), 3L, c(0, 1), 2L, ab = double(4))$ab
#> [1] 0 1 2 3

Source: R documentation: .C

Detecting writes outside an argument

A fairly common cause of crashes in .C() and .Fortran() code is writing a little beyond the end of an argument, which corrupts something else and crashes R later. options(CBoundsCheck = TRUE) (or the environment variable R_C_BOUNDS_CHECK=yes) changes how R copies the arguments: it adds 64 guard bytes at both ends of each copy and checks them on return. overrun() below has the classic off-by-one, a loop that runs to i <= *n.

/* Bug: the loop runs to i == *n, one element past the end of x. */
void overrun(double *x, int *n) {
  for (int i = 0; i <= *n; i++) {
    x[i] = 0.0;
  }
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Debugging compiled code

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB overrun.c`: the C code writes one element too many.
dyn.load(paste0("overrun", .Platform$dynlib.ext))

# options(CBoundsCheck = TRUE) makes .C and .Fortran pad each argument with 64
# guard bytes at both ends and check them when the routine returns.
getOption("CBoundsCheck")
#> [1] FALSE
options(CBoundsCheck = TRUE)
tryCatch(
  .C("overrun", c(1, 2, 3), 3L, PACKAGE = "overrun"),
  error = conditionMessage
)
#> [1] "array over-run in .C(\"overrun\") in double argument 1\n"

Source: R documentation: .C

The message names the call, the type and the argument number. It is a debugging aid: it makes every call slower, it is off by default, and it detects only writes in the guard zones.

.Fortran: subroutines

.Fortran() calls a Fortran subroutine with the same copy-and-return protocol as .C(), and the same argument table. Three rules are specific to Fortran. All the Fortran compilers R supports map symbol names to lower case, so .Fortran("loan_totals") looks for the lower-case name, and so does registration. Arguments are passed by reference, which is what Fortran expects. And the compiler decorates the symbol (often a trailing underscore); R detects the convention when it is built, which is why the R code never writes the underscore, and why C code that calls Fortran must use the macros F77_NAME, F77_CALL and F77_SUB from R_ext/RS.h, never the underscore. The help page of .Fortran() adds that a Fortran name with an underscore in it is not valid Fortran 77, and its translation can differ between compilers, so the portable advice is to use plain lower-case names (R documentation: .Fortran).

R CMD SHLIB takes .f as fixed-form Fortran (which includes Fortran 77), passing it to the compiler that R was configured with, and .f90 or .f95 as free-form. Both go to the same compiler. The manual’s advice for modern code is to use .f90, to put a requirement in SystemRequirements (for example Fortran 2018) since the standard the compiler accepts is a property of the compiler, and, when the package has several source files that use modules, to tell make the compilation order in src/Makevars, because module files are produced by compiling and make cannot see the dependency. For a module iface used by cmi.f90 and dmi.f90 the line is cmi.o dmi.o: iface.o (Writing R Extensions: Using modern Fortran code). The compile commands for Fortran are the same two lines as for C, with gfortran for the first:

R CMD SHLIB loan_totals.f90
#> gfortran -fPIC -O2 -c loan_totals.f90 -o loan_totals.o
#> gcc -std=gnu2x -shared -o loan_totals.so loan_totals.o -lgfortran -lm -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR

Source: R documentation: SHLIB

(Flags shortened, and the first line, which names the Fortran compiler and the system, omitted. The link line still uses the C driver, with -lgfortran -lm added by R’s FLIBS.)

A subroutine for .Fortran

loan_totals adds up the days beyond the loan period and counts the late loans. Every argument is declared with its intent, which is how Fortran says "input" and "output", and the sizes come from the array lengths that R passes in. The -Wall -pedantic flags of the personal Makevars compile it without warnings.

! Total and count of the days beyond the loan period, for .Fortran.
subroutine loan_totals(days, n, limit, late_total, late_count)
  implicit none
  integer, intent(in) :: n
  double precision, intent(in) :: days(n), limit
  double precision, intent(out) :: late_total
  integer, intent(out) :: late_count
  integer :: i

  late_total = 0.0d0
  late_count = 0
  do i = 1, n
    if (days(i) > limit) then
      late_total = late_total + (days(i) - limit)
      late_count = late_count + 1
    end if
  end do
end subroutine loan_totals

Source: Writing R Extensions: Interface functions .C and .Fortran

Printing, warnings, errors and random numbers from Fortran

Fortran print and write statements to the default unit are not guaranteed to appear in the R console, may not interleave with C output, and on Windows interfere with C’s own output (the manual describes how gfortran’s initialisation changes the line endings of C’s stdout and how to undo it in R_init_<pkg>). R therefore provides subroutines that print through R’s own channels: labelpr(label, nchar) prints a label, intpr1(label, nchar, var), realpr1() and dblepr1() print a labelled scalar, and intpr(), realpr() and dblepr() print a labelled array (label, nchar, data, ndata); nchar is the length of the label, or -1 for all of it. There is no check on the type: a real passed to dblepr prints nonsense. For conditions, rexit(message) signals an error and rwarn(message) a warning (messages are cut to 255 characters), and rchkusr() is the interrupt check. fortran_io.f90 uses all of them.

! Printing, a warning and an error from Fortran through R's own routines.
subroutine summarise(days, n)
  implicit none
  integer, intent(in) :: n
  double precision, intent(in) :: days(n)
  double precision :: mean

  if (n < 1) call rexit("summarise: no loans")
  if (n == 1) call rwarn("summarise: only one loan")
  mean = sum(days) / n
  call labelpr("loan summary", 12)
  call intpr1("loans", 5, n)
  call dblepr1("mean days", 9, mean)
  call rchkusr()
end subroutine summarise

Source: Writing R Extensions: Printing from Fortran

Random numbers are the other thing Fortran code must not do itself. The Fortran 90 random_number and random_seed, GNU’s rand, and the C library’s rand all keep a state that is private to the library: packages cannot initialise it safely, two packages can interfere, and the user’s set.seed() does not reach it. The manual’s rule is to use R’s generator, which a routine reaches by bracketing the draws with GetRNGstate() and PutRNGstate() and calling unif_rand() (or norm_rand(), exp_rand()), and it shows how to bind those C entry points from Fortran with iso_c_binding (Writing R Extensions: Random-number generation from Fortran). rngdemo.f90 does this without a line of C.

! Random loan lengths drawn from R's own generator (so set.seed() applies).
subroutine random_loans(n, longest, out)
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double
  implicit none
  interface
    subroutine get_rng_state() bind(C, name = "GetRNGstate")
    end subroutine get_rng_state
    subroutine put_rng_state() bind(C, name = "PutRNGstate")
    end subroutine put_rng_state
    function unif_rand() bind(C, name = "unif_rand") result(u)
      import :: c_double
      real(c_double) :: u
    end function unif_rand
  end interface
  integer, intent(in) :: n
  double precision, intent(in) :: longest
  double precision, intent(out) :: out(n)
  integer :: i

  call get_rng_state()
  do i = 1, n
    out(i) = ceiling(longest * unif_rand())
  end do
  call put_rng_state()
end subroutine random_loans

Source: Writing R Extensions: Random-number generation from Fortran

Modern Fortran through .C and bind©

For Fortran 90 and later code the help page of .Fortran() and the manual give the same advice: the most portable way is to give the subroutine a C interface with iso_c_binding and call it with .C(). With bind(C, name = "isbn_check_digit") the routine has exactly the C name given, the kinds c_int and c_double say exactly what C types the arguments are, and the compiler can check the declaration. isbn_check_digit computes the 13th digit of an ISBN from the first twelve.

! ISBN-13 check digit from the first twelve digits, callable through .C.
subroutine isbn_check_digit(digits, check) bind(C, name = "isbn_check_digit")
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_int
  implicit none
  integer(c_int), intent(in) :: digits(12)
  integer(c_int), intent(out) :: check
  integer :: i, total

  total = 0
  do i = 1, 12
    if (mod(i, 2) == 1) then
      total = total + digits(i)
    else
      total = total + 3 * digits(i)
    end if
  end do
  check = mod(10 - mod(total, 10), 10)
end subroutine isbn_check_digit

Source: Writing R Extensions: Interface functions .C and .Fortran

The script calls all four Fortran files. In the results, late_total is 49 and late_count is 3 for five loans of 14, 35, 28, 21 and 49 days against a limit of 21; summarise prints through R (the label lines and the values), warns for a single loan with the message summarise: only one loan, and stops with summarise: no loans for none (the mean of 14, 35 and 28 appears as 25.7, not 25.66667: dblepr1 uses R’s internal real-vector printer, and in this script the preceding str(res) left that printer’s number of significant digits at 3, as format() with a digits argument does too; a print() call resets it to getOption("digits"), after which the same .Fortran() call prints 25.66667, which is what was observed when the three variants were run); the draws made in Fortran are identical to ceiling(28 * runif(5)) after the same set.seed(); and the ISBN of the Le Guin entry in the catalogue has check digit 7.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB loan_totals.f90` and the other three .f90 files.
for (name in c("loan_totals", "fortran_io", "rngdemo", "check_digit")) {
  dyn.load(paste0(name, .Platform$dynlib.ext))
}
message_of <- function(expr) tryCatch(expr, error = conditionMessage)

# .Fortran: lower-case name, arguments by reference, results in a list.
res <- .Fortran("loan_totals",
  days = c(14, 35, 28, 21, 49), n = 5L, limit = 21,
  late_total = 0, late_count = 0L,
  PACKAGE = "loan_totals"
)
res$late_total
#> [1] 49
res$late_count
#> [1] 3
str(res)
#> List of 5
#>  $ days      : num [1:5] 14 35 28 21 49
#>  $ n         : int 5
#>  $ limit     : num 21
#>  $ late_total: num 49
#>  $ late_count: int 3

# Printing, warnings and errors go through R, not through Fortran I/O.
invisible(.Fortran("summarise", c(14, 35, 28), 3L, PACKAGE = "fortran_io"))
#> loan summary
#> loans
#> [1] 3
#> mean days
#> [1] 25.7
tryCatch(
  .Fortran("summarise", 7, 1L, PACKAGE = "fortran_io"),
  warning = conditionMessage
)
#> [1] "summarise: only one loan"
message_of(.Fortran("summarise", numeric(), 0L, PACKAGE = "fortran_io"))
#> [1] "summarise: no loans"

# R's generator from Fortran: the same stream as runif() after set.seed().
set.seed(2026)
from_fortran <- .Fortran("random_loans", 5L, 28, out = double(5),
  PACKAGE = "rngdemo"
)$out
set.seed(2026)
from_r <- ceiling(28 * runif(5))
from_fortran
#> [1] 20 16  4  9 16
identical(from_fortran, from_r)
#> [1] TRUE

# Modern Fortran: bind(C) makes the routine an ordinary C symbol for .C.
check_digit <- function(first12) {
  .C("isbn_check_digit",
    digits = as.integer(first12), check = 0L,
    PACKAGE = "check_digit"
  )$check
}
check_digit(c(9, 7, 8, 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1, 5))
#> [1] 7

Source: R documentation: .Fortran

Registering a Fortran routine

A registered .Fortran() routine needs a prototype in C, because the registration table is C. The prototype uses F77_NAME(loan_totals) for the name, with every argument a pointer; and a Fortran LOGICAL is declared int * in C, or better void *, because gfortran reports int_least32_t * and link-time optimisation would otherwise warn. The entry goes in an R_FortranMethodDef table, with the argument types, as the manual’s example for .C() did. R_init_<name> is named after the shared object, which is why the object is built as loantot.so.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <R_ext/RS.h>
#include <R_ext/Rdynload.h>

/* The Fortran routine as C sees it: lower-case name, every argument a pointer. */
extern void F77_NAME(loan_totals)(double *days, int *n, double *limit,
                                  double *late_total, int *late_count);

static R_NativePrimitiveArgType loan_totals_types[] = {
  REALSXP, INTSXP, REALSXP, REALSXP, INTSXP
};

static const R_FortranMethodDef fortran_methods[] = {
  {"loan_totals", (DL_FUNC) &F77_NAME(loan_totals), 5, loan_totals_types},
  {NULL, NULL, 0, NULL}
};

void R_init_loantot(DllInfo *dll) {
  R_registerRoutines(dll, NULL, NULL, fortran_methods, NULL);
  R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Registering native routines

The registration table makes the same checks as for .C(), here with Fortran’s type names in the message. The script loads the object built with R CMD SHLIB -o loantot.so loan_totals.f90 fortran_init.c.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB -o loantot.so loan_totals.f90 fortran_init.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("loantot", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
routines <- getDLLRegisteredRoutines("loantot")
routines$.Fortran
#>             numParameters
#> loan_totals             5

# Registered with argument types, so R checks them on every call.
message_of <- function(expr) tryCatch(expr, error = conditionMessage)
call_totals <- function(...) {
  .Fortran("loan_totals", ..., PACKAGE = "loantot")
}
res <- call_totals(c(14, 35, 28), 3L, 21, late_total = 0, late_count = 0L)
res$late_total
#> [1] 21
res$late_count
#> [1] 2
message_of(call_totals(c(14, 35, 28), 3, 21, late_total = 0, late_count = 0L))
#> [1] "wrong type for argument 2 in call to loan_totals"
message_of(call_totals(c(14, 35, 28), 3L, 21))
#> [1] "Incorrect number of arguments (3), expecting 5 for 'loan_totals'"

Source: R documentation: getDLLRegisteredRoutines

Character strings and logicals between C and Fortran

Two kinds of argument are not portable and need a special mention, and both are covered in the manual’s section on calling C from Fortran and vice versa.

  • Character strings. A Fortran string is an array of bytes plus a hidden length argument; a C string is NUL-terminated. Since 2019 gfortran passes the hidden length at the end of the argument list as a size_t (backported to gfortran 7 and 8), and code that ignored it broke. R defines the macro USE_FC_LEN_T and the type FC_LEN_T in Rconfig.h to match: a C routine called from Fortran declares the extra FC_LEN_T msg_len argument, and C code that calls a BLAS or LAPACK routine with character arguments (such as dgemm("N", "T", ...)) appends FCONE for every character argument, with no comma. USE_FC_LEN_T became the default in R 4.3.0, and packages that call BLAS or LAPACK with character arguments fail to install without the adjustment. The alternative is to avoid the problem, by passing integer codes instead of strings or by writing the interface with iso_c_binding (Writing R Extensions: Fortran character strings).

  • Logicals. Fortran LOGICAL has no guaranteed size. In practice it is a 32-bit integer, and int * is the traditional C equivalent, but recent gfortran says int_least32_t *. The simplest design is to pass integers and convert in a Fortran wrapper (Writing R Extensions: Fortran LOGICAL).

Passing C functions to Fortran as arguments (callbacks) depends on the two compilers agreeing on the calling convention and has failed in practice; the manual’s most portable suggestion is to convert the Fortran to C. For everything about the Fortran language and about calling it from C, C++ and Python, the Fortran Reference section added by issue #277 has the pages Interoperability with C, Calling Fortran from C, C++ and Python and BLAS, LAPACK and Numerical Libraries, and the C build and tooling page explains the compilers and linkers involved.

.External: arguments as a pairlist

.External() differs from .Call() in one respect: the C function receives a single SEXP, a pairlist whose first cell holds the name of the routine and whose remaining cells are the arguments. That removes the limit of 65 arguments and gives the C code the argument names (the "tags"), which is what makes a function with ... natural to write. The walk over the list uses the Lisp-style macros: CDR(args) is the rest of the list, CAR(args) the current argument, TAG(args) its name as a symbol (or R_NilValue), and PRINTNAME() turns a symbol into a CHARSXP. CADR, CADDR, CADDDR and so on read the first few arguments by position, and SETCAR() and its relatives modify a cell. The first cell is skipped with args = CDR(args). When registering .External() routines, the argument count is -1, which tells R not to check it.

#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* .External: the arguments arrive as one pairlist; the first cell is the name. */
SEXP total_days_ext(SEXP args) {
  args = CDR(args);
  double total = 0.0;
  for (; args != R_NilValue; args = CDR(args)) {
    SEXP el = CAR(args);
    if (!Rf_isNumeric(el)) {
      Rf_error("every argument must be numeric");
    }
    SEXP v = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(el, REALSXP));
    for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < XLENGTH(v); i++) {
      total += REAL(v)[i];
    }
    UNPROTECT(1);
  }
  return Rf_ScalarReal(total);
}

/* The tags (argument names) of the call, "" for unnamed arguments. */
SEXP arg_names(SEXP args) {
  args = CDR(args);
  int n = Rf_length(args);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(STRSXP, n));
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++, args = CDR(args)) {
    if (TAG(args) == R_NilValue) {
      SET_STRING_ELT(out, i, Rf_mkChar(""));
    } else {
      SET_STRING_ELT(out, i, PRINTNAME(TAG(args)));
    }
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return out;
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Calling .External

The R wrappers pass ... straight through. total_days() adds up any number of numeric arguments, and arg_names() returns their tags, with "" for unnamed arguments.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB external.c`.
dyn.load(paste0("external", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
total_days <- function(...) {
  .External("total_days_ext", ..., PACKAGE = "external")
}
arg_names <- function(...) {
  .External("arg_names", ..., PACKAGE = "external")
}

total_days(14, 21, 35)
#> [1] 70
total_days(1:3, c(0.5, 0.25), TRUE)
#> [1] 7.75
total_days()
#> [1] 0
arg_names(first = 1, 2, third = "x")
#> [1] "first" ""      "third"
tryCatch(total_days("a"), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "every argument must be numeric"

Source: R documentation: .External

The same job with .Call() is a one-liner in R: .Call(sym, list(...)) and a loop over the list in C. Writing R Extensions says that the .External() style is convenient but not necessary. Its value is when the C code wants the arguments and their tags without building a list first.

C++ without Rcpp

C++ code reaches R through the same C interfaces, with three differences: the entry points need C linkage, the R headers need care, and a C++ exception must never cross the boundary. The manual’s own example is a C++ library of two classes that is made callable by writing a wrapper function inside extern "C" { } and building with R CMD SHLIB (which links with the C++ compiler because there is a C++ source file); the same page warns that C++ iostreams should not be used for output, because nothing guarantees that the text reaches the R console, and that R’s own entry points (Rprintf()) should be used instead (Writing R Extensions: Interfacing C++ code). The C++ Reference page on program structure and compilation explains extern "C" and name mangling.

The three points in practice:

  • Linkage. .Call() looks up a C symbol, but the C++ compiler mangles names. A function called from R must be declared extern "C". The header files of R can be included from C++ but not inside an extern "C" block, because they include system headers.

  • Header order and R_NO_REMAP. Include the C++ standard headers before the R headers, and use the Rf_ names, because since R 4.5.0 R_NO_REMAP is always defined for C++ (an earlier section). Several R short names (length, error) collide with identifiers in the standard library.

  • Exceptions and longjmp. Rf_error() unwinds the stack with a longjmp, which skips the destructors of C++ objects between the call and the catching R frame: a std::vector or std::string alive at that moment leaks. A C++ exception must not be allowed to propagate out of an extern "C" function into R’s C code. The safe pattern is to catch all exceptions inside the C++ code, copy the message into a plain character buffer, let every C++ object go out of scope, and only then call Rf_error(). For C++ code that must run destructors when an R error unwinds the stack, R offers R_UnwindProtect() with a continuation token (R_MakeUnwindCont() and R_ContinueUnwind()), which the manual describes as suitable for C++ stack unwinding (Writing R Extensions: Condition handling and cleanup code).

cxx_median.cpp follows the safe pattern. The vector, the sort and the exception live in an anonymous-namespace function that returns a status; the extern "C" function holds only plain C data when it calls Rf_error().

#define R_NO_REMAP
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

namespace {

// All the C++ lives here; no exception leaves this function.
// Returns 0 on success, 1 after copying an error message into msg.
int median_impl(const double *x, R_xlen_t n, double *result, char *msg,
                std::size_t msg_size) {
  try {
    std::vector<double> v;
    for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
      if (!ISNAN(x[i])) {
        v.push_back(x[i]);
      }
    }
    if (v.empty()) {
      throw std::invalid_argument("no non-missing values");
    }
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    std::size_t m = v.size();
    *result = m % 2 == 1 ? v[m / 2] : 0.5 * (v[m / 2 - 1] + v[m / 2]);
    return 0;
  } catch (const std::exception &e) {
    std::snprintf(msg, msg_size, "%s", e.what());
    return 1;
  }
}

}  // namespace

// R calls C symbols, so the entry point has C linkage.
extern "C" SEXP median_cxx(SEXP days) {
  SEXP d = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(days, REALSXP));
  double result = NA_REAL;
  char msg[256];
  int status = 0;
  if (XLENGTH(d) == 0) {
    std::snprintf(msg, sizeof msg, "%s", "no non-missing values");
    status = 1;
  } else {
    status = median_impl(REAL(d), XLENGTH(d), &result, msg, sizeof msg);
  }
  UNPROTECT(1);
  if (status != 0) {
    Rf_error("%s", msg);  // only plain C data is alive here: nothing to leak
  }
  return Rf_ScalarReal(result);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Interfacing C++ code

The build is the same command with a .cpp file, and R links with g++; the C++20 option is the default of R 4.6.1. The transcript shows the two lines with the flags shortened.

R CMD SHLIB cxx_median.cpp
#> g++ -std=gnu++20 -I"<R_HOME>/include" -fPIC -O2 -c cxx_median.cpp -o cxx_median.o
#> g++ -std=gnu++20 -shared -o cxx_median.so cxx_median.o -L"<R_HOME>/lib" -lR

Source: R documentation: SHLIB

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB cxx_median.cpp`.
dyn.load(paste0("cxx_median", .Platform$dynlib.ext))
median_cxx <- function(days) .Call("median_cxx", days, PACKAGE = "cxx_median")

median_cxx(c(14, 35, NA, 21, 28))
#> [1] 24.5
median_cxx(1:4)
#> [1] 2.5

# A C++ exception was turned into an R error, with the stack unwound cleanly.
tryCatch(median_cxx(c(NA, NaN)), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "no non-missing values"
tryCatch(median_cxx(numeric()), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "no non-missing values"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Interfacing C++ code

The first error is the std::invalid_argument thrown inside the C++ function (a vector with no usable value), the second the explicit test for an empty input; R sees only the message in both cases, and no C++ object was alive when Rf_error() jumped.

Libraries are the other problem. Header-only C++ libraries (most of Boost, as packaged in the BH package; most of Armadillo, as RcppArmadillo) compile with the package and cause few problems; a library with a compiled C++ interface has a name-mangled ABI that depends on the compiler, its version and even preprocessor defines, so the package would have to be compiled exactly as the library was; and a library that uses C++ internally but offers a C interface needs the C++ runtime linked, which is done by including a dummy C++ file in src/ so that R links with the C++ compiler. The manual’s advice for libraries with both is to use the C interface (Writing R Extensions: External C++ code).

Rcpp: R objects as C++ classes

Rcpp (version 1.1.2 here) is a package of C++ headers and a small runtime that wraps R’s C API in classes. A numeric vector is a NumericVector, a list a List, a data frame a DataFrame, an R function a Function; conversion between R and C++ types happens at the boundary, PROTECT() is done by the object’s constructor and destructor, and a C++ exception thrown in your code becomes an R error. The project’s own site describes it as an interface that maps the key R data types to C++ data structures, says that it makes it easy to create a first example with cppFunction(), and reports that it is used by over 3000 packages on CRAN (Rcpp website). Rcpp is community-maintained software outside the R core, not a base package: the reference below is the package’s own documentation, the CRAN package page and the vignettes that come with it (among them the introduction, attributes, sugar and package vignettes cited below); the Rcpp Gallery (https://gallery.rcpp.org/) is community material with examples of a wide range of tasks, and is named here only as such.

What Rcpp removes

The .Call() routines of the earlier sections have a lot of ceremony that is the same each time: the SEXP signature, the coercion, the allocation, the PROTECT() and UNPROTECT() bookkeeping, the loop over REAL(x), the wrapper that attaches the attributes, the registration table and the R_init function, and the R function that calls .Call(). Rcpp attributes generate all of them. A C++ function whose signature uses Rcpp types and which is marked with // [[Rcpp::export]] is turned into an R function with the same name and arguments, including default values; the glue is generated into a pair of files in a package (RcppExports.cpp and RcppExports.R) or compiled on the fly by cppFunction() and sourceCpp().

Types, missing values and sugar

Rcpp class R object Notes

NumericVector, IntegerVector, LogicalVector, CharacterVector, ComplexVector, RawVector

the matching atomic vector

Indexed with x[i] (0-based); x.size(); x.names() or x.attr("names").

NumericMatrix, IntegerMatrix, and so on

the vector with a dim attribute

m(i, j), m.nrow(), m.ncol().

List, DataFrame

list, data frame

x["name"] or x[i] for an element; List::create(_["n"] = 1) builds a named list; DataFrame::create() builds a data frame.

Function, Environment

function, environment

f(arg) calls an R function from C++; env["name"] reads a variable.

NA_REAL, NA_INTEGER, NA_LOGICAL, NA_STRING

the missing values

NumericVector::is_na(x) tests one element; sugar’s is_na(v) is vectorised; do not compare to NA_REAL with ==.

Rcpp::stop(), Rcpp::warning(), Rcout, Rcerr

stop(), warning(), the output and error connections

stop("%d bad rows", n) takes a format; Rcout << x << std::endl is safe to use, unlike std::cout.

Source: Rcpp package documentation: Rcpp-introduction vignette

Rcpp also provides "sugar": vectorised expressions that look like R and run as C++ loops. sum(x), mean(x), ifelse(cond, a, b), is_na(x), any(...), cumsum(x), rev(x), x > limit, x - limit and many more are defined for the vector classes, so a loop can often be replaced by an expression; the sugar vignette lists them (Rcpp package documentation: Rcpp-sugar vignette).

evalCpp() and cppFunction()

evalCpp("2 + 2") compiles one C++ expression and returns its value, which is the quickest check that the toolchain works. cppFunction(code) takes the source of one function as a string, adds #include <Rcpp.h> and using namespace Rcpp;, compiles it with the C++ standard of the running R, and returns an R function. The arguments depends, plugins and includes add compile-time dependencies, plugin settings and extra includes; rebuild forces recompilation, and showOutput and verbose show what the compiler does (Rcpp package documentation: cppFunction). The script defines the two running examples, the overdue loop and the ISBN-13 check, from strings. The result of the second is compared with the C version above on the same five inputs.

library(Rcpp)
packageVersion("Rcpp")
#> [1] ‘1.1.2’

# evalCpp() compiles and runs one C++ expression.
evalCpp("2 + 2")
#> [1] 4
evalCpp("std::numeric_limits<int>::max()")
#> [1] 2147483647
evalCpp("sizeof(double)")
#> [1] 8

# cppFunction() compiles a function from a string and returns an R function.
overdue_days <- cppFunction("
NumericVector overdue_days(NumericVector days, double limit = 21) {
  NumericVector out(days.size());
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < days.size(); ++i) {
    out[i] = NumericVector::is_na(days[i]) ? days[i]
                                           : std::max(days[i] - limit, 0.0);
  }
  return out;
}")
overdue_days(c(14, 35, NA, 21, 28.5))
#> [1]  0.0 14.0   NA  0.0  7.5
overdue_days(c(14, 35), limit = 7)
#> [1]  7 28
class(overdue_days)
#> [1] "function"
args(overdue_days)
#> function (days, limit = 21)
#> NULL

# The ISBN-13 check; cppFunction() adds #include <Rcpp.h> and the namespace.
isbn13_cpp <- cppFunction("
LogicalVector isbn13_cpp(CharacterVector x) {
  LogicalVector out(x.size());
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i) {
    if (CharacterVector::is_na(x[i])) {
      continue;
    }
    std::string s = as<std::string>(x[i]);
    int n = 0, sum = 0;
    bool ok = true;
    for (char c : s) {
      if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') {
        if (n == 13) {
          ok = false;
          break;
        }
        sum += (c - '0') * (n % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 3);
        ++n;
      } else if (c == 'X' || c == 'x') {
        ok = false;
        break;
      }
    }
    out[i] = ok && n == 13 && sum % 10 == 0;
  }
  return out;
}")
isbn13_cpp(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "9780001000100", "978-0-01-100112-9", "", NA))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE

Source: Rcpp package documentation: evalCpp

The default argument of the C++ function (double limit = 21) is carried over to the R function, which args() shows. Compilation is slow the first time, because the Rcpp headers are large, and the result is cached for the session: the same code string compiles once.

sourceCpp() and a file of exports

sourceCpp("file.cpp") does the same for a file that may define many functions and helpers. It parses the file for // [[Rcpp::export]] attributes (and for RCPP_MODULE declarations), builds a shared library in a temporary directory (the build is cached, and only redone when the file changes unless rebuild = TRUE), and defines the exported functions in the calling environment. /*** R blocks in the file are R code that runs after compilation, which turns the C++ file into a self-testing script. Attributes also exist for dependencies (// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppArmadillo)]] adds the include path and flags of a package) and for plugins (// [[Rcpp::plugins(cpp17)]] requests a standard; the installed plugins include cpp11 to cpp26, openmp and unwindProtect). Its help page lists the other arguments: embeddedR, cacheDir, showOutput, verbose, dryRun and echo (Rcpp package documentation: sourceCpp). The help page also says that sourceCpp() is for one file whose only dependencies are R packages; for more files or external libraries, make a package.

loans.cpp has five exported functions. overdue_days_loop() is the C++ version of the loop of vectors.c; overdue_days_sugar() is the same job in one sugar expression; loan_stats() builds the classed list of structures.c in one expression; flag_late() takes a data frame and returns a data frame with a logical column; and mean_days() writes to Rcout, warns and stops. Nothing in the file mentions SEXP, PROTECT or .Call.

#include <Rcpp.h>
using namespace Rcpp;

// Days beyond the loan period, written as a loop; NA and NaN pass through.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericVector overdue_days_loop(NumericVector days, double limit = 21) {
  R_xlen_t n = days.size();
  NumericVector out(n);
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    if (NumericVector::is_na(days[i])) {
      out[i] = days[i];
    } else {
      out[i] = days[i] > limit ? days[i] - limit : 0.0;
    }
  }
  out.attr("names") = days.attr("names");
  return out;
}

// The same result from Rcpp sugar: vectorised expressions, as in R.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericVector overdue_days_sugar(NumericVector days, double limit = 21) {
  return ifelse(days > limit, days - limit, 0.0);
}

// A classed, named list, like the C version in structures.c.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
List loan_stats(NumericVector days) {
  NumericVector seen = days[!is_na(days)];
  List out = List::create(
    _["n"] = seen.size(),
    _["mean"] = seen.size() > 0 ? mean(seen) : NA_REAL,
    _["max"] = seen.size() > 0 ? max(seen) : NA_REAL
  );
  out.attr("class") = "loan_stats";
  return out;
}

// A data frame in, a data frame out: a logical column is added.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
DataFrame flag_late(DataFrame loans, double limit = 21) {
  CharacterVector member = loans["member"];
  NumericVector days = loans["days"];
  LogicalVector late(days.size());
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < days.size(); ++i) {
    late[i] = NumericVector::is_na(days[i]) ? NA_LOGICAL : days[i] > limit;
  }
  return DataFrame::create(
    _["member"] = member, _["days"] = days, _["late"] = late
  );
}

// Output through Rcout, a warning and an error, all as R conditions.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
double mean_days(NumericVector days) {
  if (days.size() == 0) {
    stop("no loans");
  }
  if (is_true(any(is_na(days)))) {
    warning("missing days are ignored");
  }
  NumericVector seen = days[!is_na(days)];
  Rcout << "averaging " << seen.size() << " loans" << std::endl;
  return mean(seen);
}

/*** R
overdue_days_loop(c(loan1 = 14, loan2 = 35, loan3 = NA), 21)
*/

Source: Rcpp package documentation: sourceCpp

A few lines of the script deserve a reading. The first printed block is the output of the /*** R block, echoed because echo = TRUE is the default, and printed by R as soon as the compilation finishes. The loop version keeps the names of the input (it copies the attribute) and the sugar version drops them, which is why only the first of the two printed vectors has a header line. loan_stats() returns what the C version returned, with the class attribute set from C++. flag_late() shows the data-frame round trip. And the last lines show what an error and a warning look like, which the next subsection explains.

library(Rcpp)

# Compile loans.cpp, load its exported functions, and run its /*** R block.
sourceCpp("loans.cpp")
#>
#> > overdue_days_loop(c(loan1 = 14, loan2 = 35, loan3 = NA),
#> +     21)
#> loan1 loan2 loan3
#>     0    14    NA

days <- c(loan1 = 14, loan2 = 35, loan3 = NA, loan4 = 28.5)
overdue_days_loop(days)
#> loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4
#>   0.0  14.0    NA   7.5
overdue_days_sugar(days)
#> [1]  0.0 14.0   NA  7.5
identical(overdue_days_loop(unname(days)), overdue_days_sugar(unname(days)))
#> [1] TRUE
overdue_days_loop(days, limit = 14)
#> loan1 loan2 loan3 loan4
#>   0.0  21.0    NA  14.5

stats <- loan_stats(days)
class(stats)
#> [1] "loan_stats"
unclass(stats)
#> $n
#> [1] 3
#>
#> $mean
#> [1] 25.83333
#>
#> $max
#> [1] 35
#>

loans <- data.frame(
  member = c("Ana Ruiz", "Ben Okafor", "Dev Patel"),
  days = c(14, NA, 35)
)
flag_late(loans)
#>       member days  late
#> 1   Ana Ruiz   14 FALSE
#> 2 Ben Okafor   NA    NA
#> 3  Dev Patel   35  TRUE
class(flag_late(loans))
#> [1] "data.frame"

mean_days(c(14, 35))
#> averaging 2 loans
#> [1] 24.5
withCallingHandlers(
  mean_days(c(14, NA, 35)),
  warning = \(w) {
    message("caught: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
#> caught: missing days are ignored
#> averaging 2 loans
#> [1] 24.5
err <- tryCatch(mean_days(numeric()), error = identity)
conditionMessage(err)
#> [1] "no loans"
class(err)
#> [1] "Rcpp::exception" "C++Error"        "error"           "condition"

Source: Rcpp package documentation: sourceCpp

Errors, warnings and output

Rcpp::stop("no loans") throws a C++ exception, the wrapper that Rcpp generates around every exported function catches it and calls R’s error machinery, and the result is an ordinary R error whose message is the text. It is a condition of class Rcpp::exception, C++Error, error, condition, as the last line of the output of the script shows, so tryCatch(..., error = ) handles it and conditionMessage() returns no loans. A C++ exception derived from std::exception is converted the same way, with the text of what(). Rcpp::warning() signals an R warning that withCallingHandlers() can handle, and Rcout writes through R’s output, so capture.output() and sink() see it. In the script, mean_days(c(14, 35)) prints averaging 2 loans through Rcout and returns 24.5; with c(14, NA, 35) the calling handler prints caught: missing days are ignored to the message stream and muffles the warning, and the function carries on and averages the two known values; and with numeric() the error is caught. Rcpp can also use R_UnwindProtect() so that C++ destructors run when an R error unwinds the stack, and has a plugin named unwindProtect for it.

When it does not compile

Compiler errors come out as the compiler wrote them, and R adds its own short error. broken.cpp misspells days as day inside a loop.

#include <Rcpp.h>
using namespace Rcpp;

// [[Rcpp::export]]
double total_days(NumericVector days) {
  double total = 0;
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < days.size(); ++i) {
    total += day[i];
  }
  return total;
}

Source: Rcpp package documentation: sourceCpp

The script runs sourceCpp() under tryCatch(). The compiler’s lines are written straight to the console, and the transcript keeps the part that matters: the command line is shortened (and its first line, which names the compiler and the system, is omitted), and <R_HOME> replaces the directory in the make line.

library(Rcpp)

# broken.cpp misspells a variable. The compiler's messages go to the console;
# R then signals an error whose message is short and has no paths in it.
result <- tryCatch(sourceCpp("broken.cpp"), error = identity)
#> g++ -std=gnu++20 -I"<R_HOME>/include" -I"<Rcpp>/include" -fPIC -O2 -c broken.cpp -o broken.o
#> broken.cpp: In function ‘double total_days(Rcpp::NumericVector)’:
#> broken.cpp:8:14: error: ‘day’ was not declared in this scope; did you mean ‘days’?
#>     8 |     total += day[i];
#>       |              ^~~
#>       |              days
#> make: *** [<R_HOME>/etc/Makeconf:199: broken.o] Error 1
class(result)
#> [1] "simpleError" "error"       "condition"
conditionMessage(result)
#> [1] "Error 1 occurred building shared library."

# Nothing was defined.
exists("total_days")
#> [1] FALSE

Source: Rcpp package documentation: sourceCpp

The R error is the short message that the final lines show, Error 1 occurred building shared library., and the information is in the compiler text before it; the function was not defined. Template errors can fill pages, and the useful line is nearly always the first one that contains error:. With cppFunction() the file name in the messages is a generated temporary file, since the code is a string.

Rcpp in a package: the second copy of shelf

For a package the same function is written in src/isbn.cpp, and compileAttributes() generates the glue. The steps are the ones of the C copy of shelf, with Rcpp in place of init.c. usethis::use_rcpp("isbn") adds Rcpp to the LinkingTo and Imports fields of DESCRIPTION, creates src/ with its .gitignore, writes a template src/isbn.cpp, and prints the two roxygen tags to paste. LinkingTo puts the Rcpp headers on the include path when the package is compiled. Imports makes sure the Rcpp namespace is loaded before the package’s shared object. The manual describes LinkingTo as the way to use the header files of other packages, and says that those packages must also be in Imports or Depends so that they are loaded first (Writing R Extensions: Linking to other packages). The transcript is the output of the call in a fresh copy of shelf, with the path shortened.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

The two roxygen tags go into R/shelf-package.R. @importFrom Rcpp sourceCpp is the tag that usethis prints; it makes roxygen2 write importFrom(Rcpp,sourceCpp) into NAMESPACE, which loads the Rcpp namespace with the package. @useDynLib shelf, .registration = TRUE is the tag already met.

## usethis namespace: start
#' @importFrom Rcpp sourceCpp
## usethis namespace: end
NULL

## usethis namespace: start
#' @useDynLib shelf, .registration = TRUE
## usethis namespace: end
NULL

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Managing imports and exports

src/isbn.cpp is the ISBN check as an exported C++ function. The roxygen comments are written with //' (the C++ form of #'), and compileAttributes() copies them into the generated R file, so the function is documented like any other. @export makes roxygen2 export the generated R function. The file is shorter than the C version because Rcpp supplies the loop over the vector, the allocation and the missing-value test.

#include <Rcpp.h>
using namespace Rcpp;

// Keep the digits, reject an X, weight 1 and 3 alternately.
static bool valid_isbn(const std::string& s) {
  int n = 0, sum = 0;
  for (char c : s) {
    if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') {
      if (n == 13) {
        return false;
      }
      sum += (c - '0') * (n % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 3);
      ++n;
    } else if (c == 'X' || c == 'x') {
      return false;
    }
  }
  return n == 13 && sum % 10 == 0;
}

//' Check ISBN-13 strings with C++
//'
//' `is_valid_isbn13_cpp()` gives the same answers as [is_valid_isbn13()], but
//' the check runs in C++ through Rcpp.
//'
//' @param x A character vector of ISBNs; `NA` and empty strings are allowed.
//' @returns A logical vector of the same length as `x`, `FALSE` for `NA` and
//'   for the empty string.
//' @examples
//' is_valid_isbn13_cpp(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "978-0-01-100112-9", NA))
//' @export
// [[Rcpp::export]]
LogicalVector is_valid_isbn13_cpp(CharacterVector x) {
  R_xlen_t n = x.size();
  LogicalVector out(n);
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    out[i] = !CharacterVector::is_na(x[i]) && valid_isbn(as<std::string>(x[i]));
  }
  return out;
}

src/Makevars contains a single line, the C++ standard. R’s own default would be C++20 on R 4.6; the line is shown because it is the form that a package states when it depends on a specific standard (and the SystemRequirements: C++17 field would carry the same requirement).

CXX_STD = CXX17

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using C++ code

Rcpp::compileAttributes() scans src/*.cpp for attributes and writes src/RcppExports.cpp and R/RcppExports.R. It prints what it found. This block is a fragment, not a script: it is run in the package directory and the call has no other lines.

Rcpp::compileAttributes()
#> Exports from ~/shelf/src/isbn.cpp:
#>    LogicalVector is_valid_isbn13_cpp(CharacterVector x)
#>
#> ~/shelf/src/RcppExports.cpp updated.
#> ~/shelf/R/RcppExports.R updated.

Source: Rcpp package documentation: compileAttributes

(Paths shortened.) Both files are marked "do not edit by hand", and they hold what a hand-written package would have in init.c and in the R wrapper. RcppExports.R is the R function, with the roxygen block copied from the C++ comments and a .Call() to a registered symbol whose name starts with an underscore and the package name:

# Generated by using Rcpp::compileAttributes() -> do not edit by hand
# Generator token: 10BE3573-1514-4C36-9D1C-5A225CD40393

#' Check ISBN-13 strings with C++
#'
#' `is_valid_isbn13_cpp()` gives the same answers as [is_valid_isbn13()], but
#' the check runs in C++ through Rcpp.
#'
#' @param x A character vector of ISBNs; `NA` and empty strings are allowed.
#' @returns A logical vector of the same length as `x`, `FALSE` for `NA` and
#'   for the empty string.
#' @examples
#' is_valid_isbn13_cpp(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "978-0-01-100112-9", NA))
#' @export
is_valid_isbn13_cpp <- function(x) {
    .Call(`_shelf_is_valid_isbn13_cpp`, x)
}

Source: Rcpp package documentation: compileAttributes

RcppExports.cpp holds the C-callable wrapper (_shelf_is_valid_isbn13_cpp), which converts the argument with Rcpp::traits::input_parameter, calls your function inside BEGIN_RCPP and END_RCPP (the macros that catch exceptions), and the registration: a CallEntries table and an R_init_shelf() that calls R_registerRoutines() and R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE). That is the registration section of this page, written for you.

// Generated by using Rcpp::compileAttributes() -> do not edit by hand
// Generator token: 10BE3573-1514-4C36-9D1C-5A225CD40393

#include <Rcpp.h>

using namespace Rcpp;

#ifdef RCPP_USE_GLOBAL_ROSTREAM
Rcpp::Rostream<true>&  Rcpp::Rcout = Rcpp::Rcpp_cout_get();
Rcpp::Rostream<false>& Rcpp::Rcerr = Rcpp::Rcpp_cerr_get();
#endif

// is_valid_isbn13_cpp
LogicalVector is_valid_isbn13_cpp(CharacterVector x);
RcppExport SEXP _shelf_is_valid_isbn13_cpp(SEXP xSEXP) {
BEGIN_RCPP
    Rcpp::RObject rcpp_result_gen;
    Rcpp::RNGScope rcpp_rngScope_gen;
    Rcpp::traits::input_parameter< CharacterVector >::type x(xSEXP);
    rcpp_result_gen = Rcpp::wrap(is_valid_isbn13_cpp(x));
    return rcpp_result_gen;
END_RCPP
}

static const R_CallMethodDef CallEntries[] = {
    {"_shelf_is_valid_isbn13_cpp", (DL_FUNC) &_shelf_is_valid_isbn13_cpp, 1},
    {NULL, NULL, 0}
};

RcppExport void R_init_shelf(DllInfo *dll) {
    R_registerRoutines(dll, NULL, CallEntries, NULL, NULL);
    R_useDynamicSymbols(dll, FALSE);
}
