R CMD check on this copy passed the same compiled-code checks as the C copy (foreign function calls, compilation flags in Makevars, compiled code), and added a line of its own for the C++ standard, which reads:

* checking C++ specification ... INFO
  specified C++17

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using C++ code

Two habits keep an Rcpp package healthy. Commit the generated RcppExports files, because CRAN and users compile the package without Rcpp’s tooling, and run compileAttributes() after every change of an exported signature (devtools::document() runs it as part of building, as the transcript shows); a stale RcppExports.cpp can fail to compile or to load. And do not define a second R_init_shelf() next to the generated one: two functions of the same name cannot link, so a package that uses Rcpp attributes and also has hand-written routines must register them from the generated initialiser (the attributes vignette documents the // [[Rcpp::init]] attribute for running your own initialisation code).

cpp11 and the other relatives

cpp11 (0.5.5 is installed; it was not run) is a header-only alternative in the r-lib family, with similar goals and a different design: C++11-style attributes ([[cpp11::register]]), LinkingTo: cpp11 only, copy-on-write semantics, UTF-8 everywhere, and no shared runtime library; its site describes the differences from Rcpp and how to convert (cpp11 package documentation). RcppArmadillo and RcppEigen add linear-algebra libraries to Rcpp, and RcppParallel adds threading; none of them is installed here, so they are only named. All build on the same R CMD SHLIB and LinkingTo machinery described above.

How much faster? A measurement

Whether any of this pays is a question of numbers. The script compares four implementations of the overdue-days function on a million simulated loan durations: an R for loop, the vectorised R expression pmax(days - limit, 0), the .Call() routine from vectors.c and a cppFunction() loop. bench::mark() checks that all four return the same result before timing them. Timings depend on the machine, the compiler flags and what else is running, so the script prints only the order of magnitude of each median relative to the fastest, as round(log10(ratio)); the exact ratios, which vary from run to run, are not shown. Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking explains how to measure with bench and microbenchmark.

# Built with `R CMD SHLIB vectors.c`. The same job four ways on a million
# simulated loan lengths: compare the ratios, not the seconds.
library(Rcpp)
dyn.load(paste0("vectors", .Platform$dynlib.ext))

set.seed(2026)
days <- round(runif(1e6, 1, 60))

overdue_r_loop <- function(days, limit = 21) {
  out <- numeric(length(days))
  for (i in seq_along(days)) {
    out[[i]] <- if (days[[i]] > limit) days[[i]] - limit else 0
  }
  out
}
overdue_r_vector <- function(days, limit = 21) pmax(days - limit, 0)
overdue_c <- function(days, limit = 21) {
  .Call("overdue_days", days, limit, PACKAGE = "vectors")
}
overdue_cpp <- cppFunction("
NumericVector overdue_cpp(NumericVector days, double limit = 21) {
  NumericVector out(days.size());
  for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < days.size(); ++i) {
    out[i] = days[i] > limit ? days[i] - limit : 0.0;
  }
  return out;
}")

b <- bench::mark(
  r_loop = overdue_r_loop(days),
  r_vector = overdue_r_vector(days),
  c_call = overdue_c(days),
  rcpp = overdue_cpp(days),
  min_iterations = 20
)
rel <- summary(b, relative = TRUE)
data.frame(
  expression = as.character(rel$expression),
  orders_of_magnitude_slower = round(log10(rel$median / min(rel$median)))
)
#>   expression orders_of_magnitude_slower
#> 1     r_loop                          1
#> 2   r_vector                          0
#> 3     c_call                          0
#> 4       rcpp                          0

Source: bench package documentation: mark

The result is the useful lesson. The plain R for loop is about one order of magnitude slower than compiled code here. It is byte-compiled by the JIT (see Vectorisation and Iteration), which is why the gap is a factor of ten or twenty and not larger. The vectorised R expression, which runs in R’s own compiled code, is within a factor of about three of the .Call() routine and the Rcpp function, which is the resolution of this measurement. Compiled code won over the loop and not over the right R expression. That is the usual outcome for work that a vectorised built-in can already do, and the reason to reach for C, C++ or Fortran for a loop that cannot be vectorised, and not for one that can.

Debugging compiled code

The R debugger of Debugging sees interpreted code only: browser() and debug() stop at R lines, and a .Call() is a single step. Debugging compiled code uses the tools of the language, and the manual’s chapter on debugging collects the R-specific tricks (Writing R Extensions: Debugging compiled code).

  • A crash prints a traceback. On Unix-alikes R installs a signal handler. A segmentation fault or illegal instruction prints *** caught segfault ***, the address, the R-level traceback and a menu of possible actions. Since the process may be damaged, the manual says the only really safe choices are to abort or to exit without saving the workspace.

  • Run R under the debugger. R -d gdb --vanilla starts R under gdb; on macOS the debugger is lldb (R -d lldb), and the manual has a separate section on its hurdles there. A breakpoint cannot be set in code that is not loaded yet, so the manual’s recipe is: start R under the debugger, dyn.load() or library() the shared object, send an interrupt to return to the debugger prompt, set the breakpoints, and continue with signal 0. Build with -g -O0 (in a personal Makevars) so that the debugger can step through the source; pkgload::load_all() does so by default. gdb -p <pid> attaches to a running R, and Sys.getpid() gives the pid.

  • Look at R objects from the debugger. Rf_PrintValue(s) prints an object with R’s own printing; R_PV(s) prints only objects. From gdb, p R_PV(ab) prints the object ab (Writing R Extensions: Inspecting R objects when debugging). The R FAQ has two short entries on exactly this: how to debug dynamically loaded code and how to inspect R objects when debugging (R FAQ 8.2: How can I debug dynamically loaded code? and R FAQ 8.3: How can I inspect R objects when debugging?).

  • Catch memory errors early. gctorture(TRUE) finds missing PROTECT() calls; R -d valgrind --vanilla < script.R (and --tool=memcheck --leak-check=full) checks reads of uninitialised memory and writes outside allocated blocks, with false positives that the manual explains; and R can be built with the address sanitizer and the undefined-behaviour sanitizer, which catch the same errors and some more (Writing R Extensions: Checking memory access). options(CBoundsCheck = TRUE) is the cheap test for .C() and .Fortran() overruns, shown above. Fortran has its own array bounds checking: put gfortran’s -fbounds-check in FFLAGS in the personal Makevars while checking.

  • Rprintf and the other print debugging. Still the most used. Rprintf() and Rf_PrintValue() insert into the code; a C++ std::cout should not be used for it.

  • Profiling compiled code. The R profiler (Rprof) sees a .Call() as one line. Where time goes inside it is a question for the system profilers (perf on Linux, Instruments on macOS, Very Sleepy on Windows), which the manual’s section on profiling compiled code describes, with the caveat that it is based on user reports and may not be current (Writing R Extensions: Profiling compiled code).

On Windows the equivalent is gdb from Rtools with a debug build of R and of the package (Rcmd INSTALL --debug); the details are in the R for Windows FAQ (R for Windows FAQ 8.4: How do I debug code that I have compiled and dyn.load-ed?).

Portability rules for compiled code

The manual’s chapter on writing portable packages has a section for C and C++ code, and one for Fortran, whose rules are the difference between a package that installs everywhere and one that works on the author’s machine. The points that concern code written for this page’s interfaces:

  • Never end the process. Compiled code must not call abort() or exit(), which kill the user’s R session and its unsaved work. This includes assert(), which is active unless NDEBUG is defined; R CMD INSTALL defines it, which is why the debug flags of load_all() start with -UNDEBUG. Fortran code must not call STOP or EXIT.

  • Do not write to stdout or stderr. Use Rprintf() and REprintf(), or the Fortran print routines of R. C++ and Fortran I/O should not be used.

  • Do not use the system random number generators (rand, drand48, random, Fortran random_number, the C++11 <random> library, or third-party generators such as GSL’s). Use R’s through GetRNGstate(), unif_rand() and PutRNGstate(), so that set.seed() works and packages do not interfere.

  • Mind the sizes of types. long is 32 bits on some R platforms (64-bit Windows) and 64 on most Unix. Use int, R_xlen_t, size_t or a typedef chosen by a configure test; use intptr_t for pointers stored in integers. A Fortran integer is a C int on all R platforms; a Fortran logical is not guaranteed to be.

  • Avoid -march=native and other flags that produce code for the build machine’s CPU only, and avoid sprintf() and vsprintf(), which R CMD check reports; use snprintf().

  • Include the R headers in the right order (system headers first) and never inside extern "C".

Source: Writing R Extensions: Writing portable packages

The two sections on portable code in the same chapter are Writing R Extensions: Portable C and C++ code and Writing R Extensions: Portable Fortran code. For the C standard library itself, C program structure and the C Reference pages on pointers and dynamic allocation explain the language rules that these R rules rest on.

The C API: what a package may call

R has a very large number of entry points in its executable and shared library, and most of them are not for packages. The manual divides them into three classes. The API is the set that is documented in Writing R Extensions and declared in an installed header file: packages can use it, and it is changed only after deprecation. Public entry points are declared in an installed header and exported on all platforms, but are not documented and can change without notice: they must not be used in distributed code, and their declarations will eventually be moved out of the installed headers. Private entry points are used to build R and are not declared in the installed headers at all. What R CMD check calls "non-API" is everything outside the first class.

The header files follow the same division. R.h includes the commonly used headers from R_ext/ (Arith.h, Error.h, Memory.h, Print.h, Random.h, RS.h and Utils.h); Rinternals.h declares the SEXP machinery used by .Call(); Rmath.h is R’s standalone math library; Rdynload.h (in R_ext/) is what registration needs; R_ext/Altrep.h is for packages that implement their own alternate representation of vectors, like R’s compact integer sequences; R_ext/BLAS.h and R_ext/Lapack.h declare the linear algebra routines. Headers not listed there are not part of the API, and the manual notes that Rdefines.h, an S-style macro layer, is no longer maintained (Writing R Extensions: Organization of header files).

What changed in R 4.5.0 and 4.6.0

R has been tightening the API in steps, and the NEWS files of R 4.5.0 and 4.6.0 list them. The facts that matter for a package author, in the order they happened:

  • R 4.5.0 added a section to Writing R Extensions, "Moving into C API compliance", to help authors move from non-API entry points to API ones; it will keep being updated. It made strict R headers the default, so the legacy definitions PI, Calloc, Realloc and Free are gone. It made R_NO_REMAP the default for C++. It added many functions that replace non-API ones (R_mkClosure, R_ClosureFormals, R_ClosureBody, R_ClosureEnv, R_ParentEnv, R_getVar and R_getVarEx, Rf_isDataFrame, Rf_charIsASCII and more, Rf_asRboolean). It lengthened the list of non-API entry points that R CMD check reports, and upgraded some of the NOTEs to WARNINGs, as preparation for removing the declarations and hiding the entry points where possible. A C23 compiler is selected by default where available.

  • R 4.6.0 removed declarations from the installed headers: the functions LOGICAL0, INTEGER0, REAL0, COMPLEX0 and RAW0, DATAPTR, VECTOR_PTR, Rf_isFrame (use Rf_isDataFrame), and the header R_ext/PrtUtil.h is no longer copied to the installed include directory. It marked a long list of further entry points as hidden and without declarations (ENVFLAGS, FRAME, ENCLOS, HASHTAB, IS_S4_OBJECT, LEVELS, NAMED, OBJECT, SETLENGTH, TRUELENGTH, SET_BODY and others). It upgraded to WARNINGs the check results for further non-API functions (including BODY, FORMALS, CLOENV, SET_TYPEOF, STRING_PTR, ATTRIB, SET_ATTRIB, Rf_findVarInFrame3, R_nchar and Rf_GetOption), and made the use of any non-API variable a check NOTE. And it added replacements: R_mapAttrib, R_getAttributes, R_class, R_nrow, R_ncol and a new experimental API for variable bindings.

  • R-devel (4.7.0) has no C-level entry in its NEWS section at the time of writing.

The table in the manual maps the non-API names to replacements. A selection:

Non-API use Replacement

ATTRIB(x), SET_ATTRIB, SET_OBJECT

Rf_getAttrib() and Rf_setAttrib() for one attribute; ANY_ATTRIB(x) to test for any (4.5.0); R_mapAttrib() to iterate (4.6.0); DUPLICATE_ATTRIB, SHALLOW_DUPLICATE_ATTRIB and CLEAR_ATTRIB to copy or clear.

Rf_findVar(), Rf_findVarInFrame()

R_getVar() and R_getVarEx() (4.5.0); R_existsVarInFrame() to test for existence.

BODY(), FORMALS(), CLOENV()

R_ClosureBody(), R_ClosureFormals(), R_ClosureEnv() (4.5.0).

ENCLOS()

R_ParentEnv() (4.5.0).

STRING_PTR(), DATAPTR(), STDVEC_DATAPTR()

STRING_PTR_RO() and DATAPTR_RO(); writable pointers to these are unsupported.

REAL0(), COMPLEX0()

REAL() and COMPLEX().

OBJECT(), IS_S4_OBJECT()

Rf_isObject() and Rf_isS4().

Rf_allocSExp(ENVSXP) with SET_ENCLOS

R_NewEnv(); and R_mkClosure() for closures.

R_GetCurrentEnv()

environment() in R, passed as an argument.

PRVALUE, PRCODE, PRENV, R_PromiseExpr

the binding access API of 4.6.0.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Some API replacements for non-API entry points

What happens to code that uses a non-API function

Two experiments on R 4.6.1 show the result. The first file calls ATTRIB() and Rf_findVar(), two of the entry points that the NEWS of 4.5.0 and 4.6.0 single out.

#define R_NO_REMAP
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* Both entry points are exported by libR but not declared by R 4.6's headers. */
SEXP all_attributes(SEXP x) {
  return ATTRIB(x);
}

SEXP lookup(SEXP name, SEXP rho) {
  return Rf_findVar(Rf_installChar(STRING_ELT(name, 0)), rho);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Some API replacements for non-API entry points

Neither is declared by the installed headers any more, so the compiler does not know them. On gcc 13 with the C23 option this is a warning (an implicit declaration, which C99 already disallowed), and the call is compiled as a call to a function returning int, which is wrong for a pointer. Other compilers can reject the file outright.

R CMD SHLIB nonapi.c 2>&1 | grep -E ": (warning|error):"
#> nonapi.c:7:10: warning: implicit declaration of function ‘ATTRIB’ [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
#> nonapi.c:7:10: warning: returning ‘int’ from a function with return type ‘SEXP’ {aka ‘struct SEXPREC *’} makes pointer from integer without a cast [-Wint-conversion]
#> nonapi.c:11:10: warning: implicit declaration of function ‘Rf_findVar’; did you mean ‘Rf_findFun’? [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
#> nonapi.c:11:10: warning: returning ‘int’ from a function with return type ‘SEXP’ {aka ‘struct SEXPREC *’} makes pointer from integer without a cast [-Wint-conversion]

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 4.6.0

The second experiment is a package. Package authors whose code stopped compiling because the declarations went away sometimes add the prototype themselves, which makes the file compile and hides nothing from R CMD check. probe is a deliberately wrong package of one R function and one C file, which declares Rf_findVar() by hand, does not register its routine, and sets PKG_CFLAGS = -Wall -O3.

#define R_NO_REMAP
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

/* Not declared by the installed headers any more: declared by hand. */
extern SEXP Rf_findVar(SEXP symbol, SEXP rho);

SEXP probe_lookup(SEXP name, SEXP rho) {
  return Rf_findVar(Rf_installChar(STRING_ELT(name, 0)), rho);
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Moving into C API compliance

PKG_CFLAGS = -Wall -O3

Source: Writing R Extensions: Using Makevars

The relevant part of R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual --no-tests on this package, with the other checks (all passing) left out, is below. It contains the text of the three findings. The compiled code check names the non-API call and the missing registration, says the entry point may be removed soon, and points to the two sections of the manual that matter.

* checking compilation flags in Makevars ... WARNING
Non-portable flags in variable 'PKG_CFLAGS':
  -Wall -O3
* checking compiled code ... WARNING
File ‘probe/libs/probe.so’:
  Found non-API call to R: ‘Rf_findVar’
File ‘probe/libs/probe.so’:
  Found no calls to: ‘R_registerRoutines’, ‘R_useDynamicSymbols’
This entry point may be removed soon:
‘Rf_findVar’

Compiled code should not call non-API entry points in R.
It is good practice to register native routines and to disable symbol
search.

See ‘Writing portable packages’ in the ‘Writing R Extensions’ manual,
and section ‘Moving into C API compliance’ for issues with the use of
non-API entry points.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Moving into C API compliance

(The platform header lines of the check log are not shown, and Rf_findVar was chosen because the NEWS names it among the non-API functions that R_getVar replaces; the replacement call is R_getVar(sym, rho, TRUE).) A WARNING from R CMD check does not stop a package from installing, but a package submitted to CRAN is expected to pass without WARNINGs (Publishing to CRAN covers the policy), and since R 4.6.0 the list of non-API entry points is long. The practical advice is to run R CMD check with the newest R, including R-devel, and to treat every line of "checking compiled code" as something to fix with the replacement table above. For an entry point that has no replacement, the manual’s section is the place to look first, since it is updated as the API is clarified.

Toolchain notes that affect compliance

Two toolchain facts interact with all this. First, the default C standard is C23 on R 4.5.0 and later where the compiler supports it, which rejects implicit function declarations and K&R-style definitions, so older C code needs fixing or USE_C17; and the default C++ standard is C++20 from R 4.6.0, which has removed some library features that C++17 still has (the manual gives std::uncaught_exception as an example and warns that some compilers accept removed features in C++17 mode). Second, Rtools is versioned with R: Rtools45 serves R 4.5.0 and every later R including R-devel, so the Windows toolchain of this page is the same GCC 14.2 for R 4.5 and 4.6; the version history is in the next section. R CMD config prints the compiler settings that R will use, and a CI job that checks packages on Windows, macOS and Linux with the current release and R-devel finds toolchain differences before CRAN’s checks do. How packages are checked and submitted is the subject of Publishing to CRAN.

Version notes

The entries come from the NEWS files of the corresponding releases (R NEWS and R 3.x NEWS); the dates of the Rtools releases are the R releases that adopted them.

Version Change

R 3.2.0

.C(DUP = FALSE) and .Fortran(DUP = FALSE) are ignored: the arguments are copied as DUP = TRUE would do. The help page keeps the argument for old code and says that .Call() is much preferred.

R 3.4.0

R_Calloc(), R_Realloc() and R_Free() introduced. tools::package_native_routine_registration_skeleton() added. R CMD check --as-cran notes a package that neither registers its native routines nor declares its intentions on symbol search. The styles member of R_CMethodDef and R_FortranMethodDef removed; packages that register routines for .C() or .Fortran() had to be reinstalled.

R 4.0.0

Reference counting replaces the NAMED mechanism (use MAYBE_SHARED() and related macros). The Fortran print subroutines labelpr, dblepr1, realpr1 and intpr1 added. Rf_installChar() and Rf_installTrChar() become identical.

R 4.2.0

Makevars.ucrt, Makefile.ucrt, configure.ucrt and cleanup.ucrt supported and preferred to the .win files on Windows; Rtools42 (a UCRT toolchain based on gcc 10.3) recommended. R can be built with -DSTRICT_R_HEADERS; the S-compatibility macros PROBLEM, ERROR, WARN and the like are no longer defined in R_ext/RS.h; R_Calloc and friends are preferred and used in error messages.

R 4.3.0

The default C++ standard becomes C++17 where available (C++14 or C++11 otherwise). USE_FC_LEN_T becomes the default, so C and C++ calls to BLAS and LAPACK routines with character arguments must append FCONE. Initial C++23 support. Rtools43 (gcc 12).

R 4.4.0

Rtools44 (gcc 13). The environment variable _R_CXX_USE_NO_REMAP_ makes R CMD INSTALL compile C++ with -DR_NO_REMAP. The manual dates the change that only a C++17 compiler is selected by default to this release. S4SXP becomes OBJSXP.

R 4.5.0

A C23 compiler is selected by default where available. Strict R headers are the default: PI, Calloc, Realloc and Free are removed (use M_PI, R_Calloc, R_Realloc, R_Free). R_NO_REMAP is the default for C++. The manual gains the section "Moving into C API compliance"; many API replacements are added (R_mkClosure, R_getVar, Rf_isDataFrame, Rf_asRboolean, …​); the list of non-API entry points that R CMD check reports grows, and some NOTEs become WARNINGs. C++26 support begins (from R 4.5.3 on Windows). Rtools45 (gcc 14.2).

R 4.6.0

The default C++ standard becomes C++20 where available, otherwise C++17; C++11 and C++14 are no longer supported. Declarations of LOGICAL0, INTEGER0, REAL0, COMPLEX0, RAW0, DATAPTR and VECTOR_PTR removed from the installed headers; Rf_isFrame removed; a long list of internal entry points hidden and undeclared; more non-API functions become check WARNINGs and non-API variables a check NOTE. New: R_mapAttrib, R_getAttributes, R_class, R_nrow, R_ncol, an experimental API for variable bindings, and an experimental way to allocate resizable vectors.

R-devel (4.7.0)

No C-level entry in the NEWS section at the time of writing. (Upcoming; not run.)

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 3.2.0 to 4.6.1

Registration itself is older (the manual’s example converts the splines package, which was converted in 2001), but R 3.4.0 is when R added the skeleton generator and a check NOTE for packages that did not register, and registration has been expected practice for packages with compiled code since then. The environment variable _R_CHECK_NATIVE_ROUTINE_REGISTRATION_, which makes R CMD check report packages that do not register, is documented in R Internals (R Internals: Tools).

Where to go next

  • Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking for measuring first, and for the speed-ups that need no compiled code.

  • Memory and Copy Semantics for how objects are stored, why .Call() arguments must be treated as read-only, and ALTREP compact sequences.

  • Parallel and Asynchronous Computing for running compiled code in several processes, and for the random-number rules that apply across workers.

  • Python Interop with reticulate for calling Python from R, the other way of reusing code written in another language.

  • Creating Packages, Packages, Libraries and Namespaces and Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes for DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, LinkingTo, useDynLib and the roxygen2 tags.

  • Testing with testthat for testing the R wrappers of compiled code, and Publishing to CRAN for the checks a package with compiled code must pass.

  • Debugging for the R-level tools that complement the compiled-code tools above.

  • Vectorisation and Iteration for the byte-compiler, preallocation and the apply family, which are the first things to try.

  • C Reference and C build and tooling, C++ Reference and C++ program structure and compilation, and Fortran Reference with Interoperability with C and Calling Fortran from C, C++ and Python (issue #277) for the languages themselves.
